title: Fraunhofer researchers aim to unlock the potential of lithium-metal anodes - electrive.com
content:
Researchers from two Fraunhofer Institutes are exploring new approaches to improving the performance and lifespan of battery systems. One idea is to use lithium itself as an active anode material in lithium-metal anodes, thereby achieving higher specific capacity in battery cells.
The location of the Fraunhofer IST in Braunschweig.
Image: Fraunhofer IST
The Fraunhofer Institute for Surface Engineering and Thin Films IST is collaborating with the Fraunhofer USA Center Midwest on the LIMAC project, which stands for “Amorphous Carbon Interlayers for Reliable Lithium-Metal Battery Cells”. The project has been running since September 2025 and is expected to continue until August 2028.
As part of LIMAC, the researchers are exploring new approaches to further improve batteries, with a particular focus on lithium-metal anodes. The team sees untapped potential here for developing longer-lasting battery cells, particularly regarding the interface between the lithium-metal anode and the (solid) electrolyte. According to the researchers, the stability of this interface is essential for achieving more reliable and durable battery cells.
To stabilise this interface, the Fraunhofer experts are introducing thin amorphous carbon layers. In the first step, these layers are deposited onto copper current collectors using an innovative Laser-Arc PVD process. “The coated materials will then be tested in battery cells and compared with reference cells,” the researchers explain. The goal is to determine which properties of the interlayers are critical for achieving the most stable interface within the battery cell. It is clear that the stabiliser is intended to enable the lithium contained in the cell to serve as an active anode material itself.
In addition to technical performance, the project also examines the ecological perspective and the future transferability to larger cell formats. “On the one hand, a life cycle assessment (LCA) will be used to examine relevant material and energy flows as well as the environmental impacts of the approach; on the other hand, a concept for scaling the technology to larger pouch cells will be developed simultaneously,” the team explains. In this way, the project combines material development and cell research with ecological evaluation and initial considerations for future scaling.
The potential added value for manufacturers is clear: more powerful and longer-lasting lithium-metal batteries could reduce the weight of electric vehicles while maintaining high energy densities. However, LIMAC is still at the stage of basic research.

title: How Gotion Built Its 40 GWh Gigafactory in Illinois
content:
Stationary Batteries
Battery Applications
Battery Manufacturing
Experts from Epstein and Gotion explain how a former Kmart distribution center in Illinois became a battery gigafactory by overcoming major challenges.
October 23, 2026
6 Min Read
How Gotion built its 40 GWh gigafactory in Illinois
Maria Guerra
At The Battery Show North America, David Scott, Senior Vice President and Director of Professional Services at
, and Mohamad Zeitoun, Head of Market Management at
, came together to speak publicly about developing Gotion’s 40 GWh gigafactory in Illinois. Gotion also won a
2026 Battery Award
in the Grid-scale Energy Storage Project of the Year category. Their conversation offered a rare inside look at the project’s journey, from identifying and adapting the right facility to overcoming design, infrastructure, and power challenges. One of the clearest themes to emerge was how difficult it has been to adapt Gotion’s established battery manufacturing model from China to the US market.
Adapting a Chinese battery model to the US
After failing to build a
gigafactory in Michigan
, Gotion’s gigafactory success project in Illinois still shows how difficult it is to bring a battery manufacturing model from China into the US. Scott said the team began by studying Gotion’s facilities in China. “We went to Hefei, China to look at the facilities that were really the template for this facility,” he said. But he also made clear that using that template in the US came with immediate complications. “One of the big challenges that we had… [was] the template that they’ve used in China, and translate that… using US codes and standards.” He added, “It’s a challenge… cultural shift challenge. It’s a paradigm challenge.”
Related:
Should Batteries Be Beautiful? Torus Thinks So.
That gap between the Chinese model and the American context shaped the entire project. Scott put it simply: “Sometimes the way things are done in China aren’t done the same way in the US.” Gotion also imported much of its equipment and vendor base from China to preserve the original production concept. Scott said that “probably 75 to 80% of the equipment and the vendors have come from China,” including piping, dust collection systems, ductwork, and process equipment. That created continuity, but it also created coordination challenges when those systems had to be installed and made to work inside an existing US facility.
A layout strategy built around a long, linear process
One of the biggest design issues was layout. The team was not starting with a purpose-built battery plant. It was converting a former Kmart distribution building into a lithium battery manufacturing facility, which created challenges.
Scott described the building as “1,200 feet by 1,550 feet,” and said that production lines take up nearly that whole 1,200 linear feet. Usually, process lines include mixing, cutting, slitting, injection, and grading, which becomes a challenge when the line effectively stretches the entire length of the building. In a repurposed warehouse facility, it becomes even harder because manufacturing flow must be merged with egress and life-safety rules.
Related:
Second-Life EV Batteries Are Cutting Grid Storage Costs in Half, Says B2U CEO
When talking about exit access travel distance, Scott noted that “under S-1, your travel distance is 400 feet,” which is difficult to manage in such a large industrial footprint. “Everything is not linear,” he said. “We need to get from this point in the room around this piece of equipment, and we need to exit.” One of the project’s most important design moves was using existing firewalls as “horizontal barriers,” allowing the team to break the facility into code-compliant zones.
Safety and code compliance in a battery manufacturing industry
Battery manufacturing also brings perception challenges, especially in communities and agencies that are still getting used to the industry. Scott said, “There is an overemphasis on the concerns of battery safety,” and added that “sometimes those get blown out of proportion.”
He explained that the team spent time helping the fire department understand where battery-specific hazards actually emerge in the process. “The battery that we’re going to make… isn’t a battery until we’re three-fourths of the way down the supply chain,” he said. Before that point, “everything that we’re doing, we could be doing in any other manufacturing space.”
Related:
Report: Data Center Battery Storage Market to Reach $4.27 Billion by 2035
That distinction matters because a battery plant is not a uniform hazard environment; risk changes along the production line. Scott described “regulatory and safety compliance” challenges tied to “changing the building… from a warehouse storage into… lithium battery manufacturing.” In other words, the team was not just fitting equipment into a building. It was redefining the building’s identity under US codes.
Power and utilities demands and site challenges. Courtesy of Maria Guerra.
Mobile substations as a critical bridge
A major reason the project could move forward was the use of mobile substations. For a gigafactory, power is not a background issue. It determines whether production can start, whether equipment can be tested, and whether the project can transition from construction into operations.
Zeitoun explained that pack production may use 10MW to 30MW, with laser welders consuming the most. But once the facility moves further into cell manufacturing, demand rises. For example, ovens in cell manufacturing that can remove moisture, cure binders, etc., often consume roughly 30% to 40% of the total factory power. That meant the factory could not simply wait for permanent infrastructure to arrive at the end of the process.
Instead, the team worked with the state of Illinois to secure temporary power capacity. “We talked to the governor’s office and said, ‘Can we get something over about 35 megawatts to allow us to do the pack production and then also start some of the cell manufacturing?’” Zeitoun said. “They pulled one of these mobile substations.” That temporary asset was essential because it bridged the gap between current utility limits and future electrical buildout.
Energy storage units as power strategy
The longer-term solution is even more interesting. Zeitoun said Gotion is beginning to use its own products as part of the plant’s operating strategy. “What we started doing now… is using what we make, which is energy storage system containers,” he said. These units range from “5MWh to 20MWh,” and the plan is to place them outside the building and connect them to operations.
Their purpose is to shift and manage demand. “Now we can… peak shave,” Zeitoun said, storing energy during lower-demand periods and using it when production lines start up in the morning. He added that the company is planning a 360 MWh battery energy storage system capacity on site.
Taken together, the challenges described by Scott and Zeitoun show that building a gigafactory in the US is not simply a matter of importing equipment or replicating an existing model from China. It requires rethinking design, safety, infrastructure, and power strategy to fit a very different operating environment.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre is handed the first metal made from HalZero electrolysis technology by Hanne Simensen, Executive Vice President Hydro Aluminium Metal. Credit: Anders Vindegg / Hydro
Supply Chain Digital takes a look at the top stories of the week, including record-breaking stats from o9, announcements from UPS and projects from PepsiCo
Hydro Produces First Aluminium Using HalZero
Hydro has announced that it has successfully produced the first aluminium from aluminium chloride at its Herøya research and test facility in Porsgrunn, Norway on 19 October. The technological achievement represents a significant step towards validating its patented aluminium production process, HalZero.
The long-term ambition is to eliminate CO2 emissions from both electrolysis and anode production, releasing oxygen instead of CO2.
“This is an important milestone for Hydro and Norway’s technology and research communities, and a significant step forward in the development of HalZero,” says Eivind Kallevik, President and CEO of Hydro.
UPS Expands Capabilities Across Asia Pacific Logistics
UPS is maintaining its competitive edge within global logistics, with its ongoing expansion and newest addition to its network.
The logistics company has opened a new hub at Clark International Airport in the Philippines, increasing opportunities across more than 1,100 global trade lanes.
Through this, the company will be seeing greater efficiency and its customers will have more options to choose from.
Maersk, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and a local supplier conducted a bunkering operation of a 5,000t stem of ethanol on 17 October 2026. Credit: MPA
Maersk Singapore Ethanol Bunkering Sets Technical Milestone
Maersk completed an ethanol bunkering operation at the Port of Singapore on 18 October 2026.
The bunkering operation saw a 5,000 tonne stem of bioethanol bunkered aboard
Maersk’s container vessel
Maersk Halifax at the Pasir Panjang terminal at the Port of Singapore.
The operation represented a number of firsts: it was the first ethanol bunkering operation to be concluded at the Pasir Panjang terminal, and the first ethanol bunkering operation for a vessel retrofitted to ethanol operation for Maersk. The 5,000t stem of ethanol was also the largest volume of ethanol to be bunkered globally to date.
PepsiCo Greenhouse Programme APAC 2026: The IMPACT Edition aims to prepare pilots for deployment into day-to-day operations. Credit: PepsiCo

The company has signed five letters of intent with returning alumni to explore future integration across PepsiCo’s Asia Pacific operations.
“What's exciting about these solutions is that many of them can support both sustainability goals and business resilience at the same time,” Ashley Brown, Chief Sustainability Officer at PepsiCo APAC, tells Supply Chain Digital. “That's where we see the greatest opportunity for the APAC Greenhouse program.”

title: Chinese EVs found back door into Western car markets – at 40% off MSRP
content:
Used EVs
Jo Borrás
| Oct 24 2026 - 7:04 am PT
The dumb oil war in Iran is driving up the cost of just about everything
, including new cars. That’s giving Chinese EVs a huge advantage over Western “legacy” car brands already lagging in tech and struggling with affordability – and those legacy brands about to have a whole
new to them
problem on their hands:
USED Chinese EVs
Western automakers have leaned on protectionist trade policies to keep cheaper Chinese rivals at bay, placing strict limits on the number of new Chinese cars allowed in and hefty tariffs on new battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) are as high as 45.3% in the EU. That supply limitation is, of course, ratcheting up demand for the high-tech, low-cost Chinese machines,
and buyers in Europe and Canada are finding that
Chinese EVs
– which offer comparable tech to the newest Western EVs, a price tag up to 40% lower than their already low MSRPs, and which are
subject to the same protectionist import duties – are a workable alternative.
According to data shared by importers/exporters
China EV Marketplace
), pre-owned vehicle sales to EU customers grew 280% year over year, with sales climbing to 7,900 units through September.
“Tariffs have already weakened demand for new Chinese BEVs among our European customers. We expect the hybrid import cap to put pressure on new PHEV sales too,”
CEVM COO Jakub Geršl told
CarNewsChina
. “Pre-owned cars are exempt from the additional BEV tariffs and from the new hybrid (PHEV) quota. That is why we are making pre-owned vehicles the main focus of our European business.”
Relentless progress
A shipment of Lotus Cars arrives in Canada; via Geely.
CEVM has more than 2,600 used Chinese EVs on its website as I type this, and their inventory is refreshed almost daily with fresh pre-owned examples of cars from brands like BYD, Geely, Zeekr, and others – and the company claims its prices are about 40% below the original price (MSRP) on average.
“Lower new-car prices put pressure on pre-owned prices as well,” Geršl adds. “Our Shanghai-based team searches for those opportunities. We regularly find cars with around 6,000 km on the clock priced 40% below their original Chinese list price.”
That price reduction is driven by a number of factors, including the relentless march of technological progress, the flood of new and updated EVs coming out of Chinese car brands, and a burgeoning domestic Chinese car culture that values newness above all else. If you’re reading between the lines there, I think you’ll find that that means more low-mileage, low-price, high-tech, and high-value Chinese EVs are coming to the West – and probably a lot sooner than brands like VW,
who are struggling to compete as it is
, would want.
And that’s the real problem – whether you agree with him or not,
Elon Musk will tell you that technology and markets move faster than legislation
, and once consumers go electric,
precious few of them ever go back to gas or diesel
, regardless of what that dude filming himself wearing PitVipers in the drivers’ seat of his pickup and your racist uncle on Facebook are telling you.
Let us know if you agree, and if you’d give a used Chinese EV a chance if one showed up at your local
, in the comments.

title: NHTSA proposes cyan lights for robotaxis, following Mercedes/China
content:
The NHTSA has proposed using cyan-colored lights to identify vehicles operating autonomously, along with other additions to get ready for autonomous vehicles.
As the autonomous vehicles start to spread on US roads, questions have come up about how to deal with these new driverless vehicles.
One question involves emergency response – not only do the vehicles need to be prepared to respond to emergency personnel, those personnel need to recognize when a car is operating autonomously. A police officer needs to know that nobody’s in the driver seat, or an emergency responder needs to know that if there’s nobody in the driver’s seat, that’s not necessarily because there’s a missing driver somewhere who needs rescue.
These are just some of the reasons one might want to know whether a car is operating autonomously, but as of yet, there is no standardized messaging to suggest that a vehicle is doing so.
This week, NHTSA proposed an answer. In a draft proposal released Friday, it suggested a whole new color for vehicle lamps, cyan, to signal autonomous operation.
The proposal was actually first put forward by Mercedes, alongside its DRIVE PILOT level 3 driver assist system. This is the first true hands-free system offered in the US, which allows drivers to forgo responsibility for the car under certain conditions, and let the car truly drive itself. This differs from systems like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, which is actually only a “level 2” system, where the driver is still responsible when the system is on.
We tried Mercedes’ system out in Santa Monica traffic, and were impressed at how quickly we adjusted to our temporary robotic chauffer.
When we saw that system, we also saw Mercedes’ proposal for lighting: cyan lights around the exterior of the vehicle, denoting autonomous operation.
Unfortunately our demo was on a bright sunny day (a necessity to operate the level 3 system, which doesn’t run at night or in bad weather), so the lights didn’t pop as much as they might have in lower light, but you get the drift.
Mercedes trialed the system in California for two years, and it seems the NHTSA is happy with the results, since it is proposing to take the idea national (after input from the SAE, which also likes the idea of using cyan).
The new draft regulation would allow for optional inclusion of cyan lights, but would not require them. So, it’s entirely possible that automakers would decide to save the small cost that it would take to engineer and include these lights.
But by putting the idea out into the regulations, it gets everyone thinking about a future where this color might be required (and I could see that requirement coming quite quickly) – so automakers are likely to start thinking of where these lights would go, and including them, since LEDs don’t really cost anything anyway.
The regulation states that the lights should turn on when the car is operating autonomously, and turn off when it isn’t – they should never be on when a driver is actively driving the vehicle. They should all turn on and off simultaneously, and they should be visible from any angle, with markers on the front, sides and rear, all at least 15 inches off the ground.
China just announced essentially the same regulation earlier this week. The country released a draft standard that would take effect in 2028, is optional, and uses turquoise as its proposed color. This, too, was a reaction to the proliferation of lights on autonomous vehicles in China, and the government has asked automakers to stop doing their own thing and instead follow the new standardized system.
The NHTSA’s draft regulation covers several other aspects of autonomous vehicle operation, mostly by updating Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) rules to allow some flexibility for certain operations that won’t be used by autonomous vehicles.
For example, cars are required to have a turn signal that turns off automatically after the steering wheel turns beyond a certain threshold and then returns back to neutral. That wouldn’t apply to cars without steering wheels, so the updated rules delete that requirement for autonomous cars. It also changes certain headlight requirements for more design flexibility.
Electrek’s Take
While I’ve got a lot to say about the corrupt reality TV character running the DoT, and how he’s trying to raise your energy costs and kill children on bicycles, this autonomous vehicle regulation is a long time coming and is needed.
There are still some careerists in the NHTSA who take their job seriously, and are pushing regulations like this, and we can be thankful that not all of them have been forced out by the rampant corruption the US is seeing right now.
That said, the loosening of rules for autonomous vehicles is something we need to keep our eye on. Certain things, like allowing reasonable changes to FMVSS rules for things that really make no sense for an AV (like the turn signal change, or various required driver displays), are totally reasonable.
But it’s also hard not to look at this and say, well, could the guy who has given hundreds of millions in bribes to try to cancel investigations against him and wants to sell you an unusable car without a steering wheel be behind any of this?
Top comment by Philip234
NHTSA would be better off just shutting down and copy-paste regulations from EU on vehicle safety and China on autonomy. Both require more stringent safety and it would align the US with the larger markets.
Sadly, the US regulators are no longer independent thanks to the rampant political corruption and they are no longer sufficiently staffed to develop and implement regulations. Outsource development and become an agency that enforces the regulations developed in the more advanced markets.
After all, that steering-wheel-less car was subject to an immediate NHTSA investigation when it was suddenly put into service without forewarning, with the NHTSA pointing out myriad problems. Changing the rules after the fact to accompany a vehicle that already violated them doesn’t set great precedent.
So… we can be happy for the adaptation to new technology, but still need to ensure that safety is the North Star, rather than Mr. Musk’s fantasies. We have no specific reason in mind to oppose this specific regulation, but an environment so rife with corruption does not foster trust with the general populace, so here we are.
The rule will soon be posted for public comment, for a 30 day period, under docket NHTSA-2026-1519 at www.regulations.gov.

title: EGO Commercial expands ZTR line with mowers, blowers, and trimmers
content:
Electric Power Tools
e-quipment highlight
EGO Power
Jo Borrás
| Oct 24 2026 - 4:59 am PT
EGO Power garage; made using AI.
EGO Power’s commercial group showed up at this week’s EQUIP Expo with a trio of new zero-turn riding mowers,
a commercial-grade 780 CFM leaf blower
, and a heavy-duty 16.5″ trimmer built for the 56V PGX battery system. And,
with incentive programs designed to help landscapers make the switch to electric popping up all over
, the timing couldn’t be better.
Visitors to the EGO Commercial booth this week were greeted with a trailer-load of new, professional-grade electric landscaping equipment, an expanded interchangeable battery ecosystem, and a connected equipment platform meant to help landscapers manage their energy needs now and prepare them for future growth. In other words:
it was a lot
“Our focus at EGO Commercial is developing products that deliver the performance professional landscapers demand so they can maximize productivity and minimize downtime,” said Tim Baker, vice president of product at EGO parent company, Chervon. “From professional-grade mowing and handheld equipment to scalable charging and fleet management, every component is designed to work together so landscaping businesses can get more from their battery investment across their entire operation.”
The official copy gets into some of the basic specs of the new EGO Commercial mowers, walking prospective buyers through the basics:
Commercial sit-down ZTR
: Built for demanding commercial mowing, the sit-down ZTR delivers up to 44 gas-equivalent horsepower and mowing speeds of up to 12 mph, with durable 48-, 54- and 60-inch deck options. Powered by up to four removable, high-capacity batteries, the mower features an onboard 700-watt DC-to-DC charger, allowing professionals to recharge handheld EGO 56V ARC lithium batteries directly in the field.
Commercial stand-on ZTR
: The stand-on ZTR delivers up to 44 gas-equivalent horsepower and mowing speeds of up to 12 mph, with durable 48-, 54- and 60-inch deck options. Equipped with up to four removable, high-capacity batteries, the mower features an onboard 700-watt DC-to-DC charger for convenient hand-held battery charging.
Commercial Compact Stand-On ZTR

title: Renewable Energy India Expo 2026: Three key takeaways - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
India’s largest renewable energy trade show returned to Greater Noida, outside of Delhi, this week. At the three day event, pv magazine took in a national solar industry that has reached enormous proportions, and continues to grow with huge investments still going into building new solar installations, upgrading grids and adding, and ramping up a localized supply chain for many of the components these projects rely on.
Mark Hutchins
24 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
REI Expo
India’s solar manufacturers are largely focused on TOPCon cell technology
India’s solar and energy storage industry has grown to massive proportions, reflected in the more than 54,000 visitors that descended on Greater Noida’s India Expo Center this week for Renewable Energy India Expo (REI) and the Battery Show India, and the more than 1,000 exhibitors that filled the center beyond its capacity, with temporary buildings added and exhibits flowing out into the car park.
After three days navigating the halls and meeting with companies from up and down the solar supply chain, pv magazine has these three key takeaways from REI 2026.
Survival of the biggest
Previous years at REI saw a PV industry highly focused on bringing module assembly to India. And now, analysts estimate the country has more than 200 GW of annual module capacity – far beyond its expected demand for 50-60 GW of PV installations per year out to 2030.
This has many predicting a market shakeout beginning in 2027, where manufacturers operating module capacity only will struggle to find demand, and also to source cells since the country extended its domestic content requirements to the cell sector earlier this year.
Many manufacturers at the show were keen to emphasize their ability to supply “domestic content requirement” modules. Nonetheless, 2027 may be a difficult year for some. India’s market is led by those companies that have been able to invest early in building out local cell manufacturing capacity – expected to reach 80 GW by the end of 2027.
Quality is also emerging as a key differentiator as module manufacturing heads into a highly competitive period. And speakers at pv magazine’s Insight session on day 2 were keen to emphasise their sophisticated quality control procedures, as well as work to ensure their modules are prepared specifically for the varying and often harsh climates found in India.
Atanu Samanta of Kosol Energie, Pirmin Preis of ISC Konstanz, Sai Charan Kuppli of Premier Energies and Mahesh Murthy of Waaree Energies joined a panel discussion moderated by pv magazine. | Image: pv magazine
The next step for India’s domestic content plans is adding solar wafers to the list of components that must be produced in India for modules used in projects receiving government assistance. And many of those same companies are now announcing plans to produce wafers locally as well – Saatvik, Grew, Solex, Zetsol, Navitas, Reliance, Adani, and more all shared plans to have wafer production up and running by the time policy takes effect in 2028.
While India’s ambition to host the entire PV supply chain is clear, opportunities for international collaboration are still there, with some manufacturers happy to discuss OEM deals in place with established manufacturers in China, as well as collaboration with technology suppliers in Europe and the United States.
India’s PV market has long been utility-scale led, and so favored those with the ability to supply and operate at megawatt or even gigawatt scale. Many manufacturers that pv magazine spoke with this year, however, also expressed optimism about the country’s commercial and industrial sector, where companies are keen to secure long term energy prices away from the grid, and to meet decarbonization goals. Several also spoke of new demand from the residential sector, and particularly the opportunity that adding residential batteries to the PV offering will add in the next year or two.
Totally TOPCon
Virtually all of India’s cell manufacturing buildout is focused on tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) technology. And those manufacturers expect this to remain the mainstream for several years at least.
Reliance Industries, which is building out a 20 GW supply chain focused on heterojunction technology, is the most notable exception. A few others still have older passivated emitter rear cell (PERC) production lines that they expect to be able to keep running for a few more years at least. And mentions of back contact were few, and confined to those sourcing cells from abroad or working on OEM deals with Chinese manufacturers.
Most manufacturers told us that they have perovskite tandem cells on their radar, but still see this technology as at least five years away from commercial. Others though, including Grew Solar, Navitas Solar, Rayzon Solar and INA Solar, are partnering with US-based perovskite producer Caelux, and plan to have hybrid perovskite-silicon modules commercially available in India by 2028.
Indian PV manufacturers are focused on cell capacity this year, and beginning investments in wafer as well. | Image: pv magazine
One stop shops
Moves to cover more of the supply chain also extend far beyond the cell and wafer segment. Other module components like encapsulant films, glass, aluminum are not covered by domestic content requirement, nonetheless several manufacturers are investing in capacity to produce these locally as well, while Indian solar glass maker Borosil is itself expanding into module production.
Many manufacturers are also expanding into projects sector, developing and building projects with their own modules. Waaree Energies and other companies more known in the PV module sector have begun producing inverters. Others including Gamechange Energy and Delta Electronics are expanding into production of transformers and other system components in India.
Some on the projects side of the industry said that the shock of the domestic content requirement for cells has pushed prices upward and temporarily slowed plans for new projects, all expect this to be a short-term issue though as India demonstrates that it has the scale and the capital to support an energy system based on components made in India.

title: Gritt Robotics brings AI-assisted robotics to bolster shrinking solar workforce - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
California firm working with top EPCs to install six million solar panels in the next two years.
Michael Puttré
24 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Utility-scale
Robots are most effective in laboratories or controlled environments, such as a factory floor. When robots are required to automate tasks outdoors, the range of applications narrows with the number variables encountered. For this reason, construction sites remain labor-intensive locations resistant to robotics.
Solar construction sites may admit more automation than other sorts because of the regularity and essentially two-dimensional aspect of their layouts. Placement of heavy bases and even tracker tubes have been automated to some degree on many utility-scale solar projects for years. A key goal of these implementations is to have robots take over the more arduous tasks of materials transport and repetitive placement in all weather conditions.
More recently, robotics startups have been developing technologies for placing panels and even performing more dexterous finishing tasks. Some of these companies have received significant
investment
contracts
with engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) firms.
California-based Gritt Robotics focused squarely on large-scale solar construction for its approach to retrofitting commercial construction equipment with computer control featuring AI for improved flexibility and even site management support. Gritt recently announced it has
deployed
its robotic construction systems at solar job sites run by EPC Burns & McDonnell. In all, the company says it is it’s working with three top-10 solar EPCs to install six million solar panels in the next two years with a capacity of about 2.8 GW.
Puneet Puri, co-founder and CEO of Gritt, told
pv magazine USA
that large-scale solar sites have been an excellent proving ground for the company’s AI-assisted robotics technology.
“Outdoors is hard,” Puri said. “Outdoors, there’s going to be a lot of variability. Our thesis is that solar offers an example of a construction site where there are a lot of physically demanding, repetitive steps and materials transport that can be automated. At the same time, because it is outside, we can address aspects of a dynamic environment. We can build an intelligence layer that understands the challenges on the site, like trenches are open, people are moving through, materials may have snow or rain or dust on them, the light changes.”
Thus, large-scale solar construction has that right combination of regularity and variability where a robot with the proper common representation layer that can be trained for individual tasks under varying conditions. Ultimately, Gritt intends to apply the lessons learned from solar sites to data center construction and other infrastructure projects.
At the same time, Puri says solar has many repetitive tasks beyond heavy lifting that can be applied to other types of construction, such as tying rebar, applying fasteners, or attaching cables. It is all a matter of training. An aspect of Gritt’s software driven, AI learning approach is that nearly any type of construction vehicle or robotic arm can be retrofitted to perform specialized tasks autonomously.
“Caterpillar and Bobcat know how to build good vehicles,” Puri said. “For that matter, Kawasaki, FANUC, and KUKA know how to build good robots. Why should we reinvent the base platforms, which in many cases have been working in the harshest environments? We focus on writing the right brain to control them to do their jobs safely and repetitively.”
In terms of training, Vishal Dugar, co-founder and chief technology officer at Gritt, told
pv magazine USA
that like human workers, AI builds the ability to understand patterns, certain similarities of how to operate from one job site to another.
“When a person learns how to use a particular tool on one job, those skills remain constant,” Dugar said. “The AI also learns. It identifies all the similar patterns that it can reuse to make learning the next job that much faster.”
Puri and Dugar are alumni of the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU). Other members of Gritt’s leadership team also hail from CMU, or from MIT or other centers of automation research and practical application. There was a time when robots out in the field had to be purpose-built and shepherded by specialists to perform specific functions, whether descending into an Antarctic volcano or surveying the ruins of Chernobyl. Now, robots are on the cusp of taking on a wide variety of tasks guided by tutors rather than wrangled by technicians.
As indicated earlier, if the company views unstructured construction environments as the new frontier for physical AI, large-scale solar projects are proving to be an excellent proving grounds. It’s not just the relatively straightforward process of building out arrays. The industry is signaling a need for workers and warns of a growing shortage. According to recent
industry reports
, there is a shortfall of 53,000 workers needed to complete ongoing projects. Some estimate that 41% of construction workers nationwide will retire by 2031.
With competition for construction workers heating up, EPCs face a need to move and support personnel for projects in remote locations where accommodations are scarce. If this is the case for large-scale solar projects, it will also apply to data centers and other infrastructure projects facing opposition in populated areas.
“The mission of the company is to help civilization build infrastructure rapidly,” Puri said. “A big part of our vision is to help create the workforce of tomorrow. It’s not the same workforce that is doing the same things in the same way. It’s people who can use the tools we are developing to amplify what they’re able to do.”

title: Italy deploys 4.83 GW of PV in January-September - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Italy connected 4.83 GW of new solar capacity in the first nine months of 2026, bringing cumulative installed capacity to 48.35 GW at the end of September. Utility-scale projects accounted for 46% of new additions, while the country’s cumulative battery storage capacity approached 20 GWh, according to new statistics from Italia Solare.
Sergio Matalucci
24 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
A rooftop PV system in Venice, northern Italy
Italy installed 4.83 GW of new solar capacity in the first nine months of 2026, with 147,632 new systems connected to the grid, according to data released by industry association Italia Solare. As a way of comparison, the newly installed PV capacity for the January-September period in 2025 was 4.08 GW across 161,962 new installations
The additions brought the country’s cumulative installed PV capacity to 48.35 GW across 2,314,113 systems at the end of September 2026.
The figures are based on Italia Solare’s analysis of data from Italian grid operator Terna’s Gaudì database, covering PV and energy storage installations connected to the grid through the third quarter of 2026.
In the third quarter alone, Italy connected 1.74 GW of new PV capacity, up 5% from 1.65 GW in the second quarter and 37% from 1.27 GW in the third quarter of 2025. The number of new connections also increased, rising from 38,660 in the second quarter to 58,459 in the third quarter, a 51% quarter-on-quarter increase.
The data indicate that the Italian solar market continued to expand in the third quarter, with utility-scale projects accounting for the largest share of new capacity.
Utility-scale solar accounts for 46% of new capacity
Utility-scale projects dominated the Italian PV market in the first nine months of 2026, accounting for 2.24 GW of newly connected capacity across 473 installations, or approximately 46% of the total.
The commercial and industrial (C&I) segment followed with 1.70 GW across 11,905 installations, representing 35% of new capacity. Residential installations of up to 20 kW accounted for 897 MW across 135,254 systems, equivalent to approximately 19% of newly connected capacity.
All three market segments recorded year-on-year growth in the third quarter.
Utility-scale installations of 1 MW or more reached 858 MW, compared with 457 MW in the third quarter of 2025, representing an 88% year-on-year increase. Projects between 1 MW and 10 MW accounted for 394 MW, while installations exceeding 10 MW contributed 464 MW.
The C&I segment added 543 MW in the third quarter, up 9% from 500 MW in the corresponding period of 2025. Residential installations reached 341 MW, compared with 312 MW a year earlier, an increase of approximately 9%.
The figures show that large-scale projects remained the main driver of capacity growth, although residential and C&I installations also recorded gains.
Sicily leads solar additions, Lombardy tops installation count
Sicily recorded the largest amount of newly connected PV capacity in the first nine months of 2026, with 686 MW. Lombardy followed with 644 MW, ahead of Piedmont (498 MW), Veneto (463 MW), Emilia-Romagna (443 MW), and Lazio (432 MW).
Sicily’s leading position was largely driven by utility-scale developments. Of the 686 MW connected in the region, 476 MW came from projects exceeding 10 MW. Lombardy, by contrast, recorded particularly strong activity in the C&I segment, which accounted for 405 MW of its new capacity. Lombardy also led the country in the number of new PV connections, with 22,999 installations, followed by Veneto (18,099), Emilia-Romagna (13,405), and Sicily (11,653).
The regional figures highlight the different development patterns across Italy, with large-scale solar projects driving capacity additions in southern regions and smaller commercial and industrial systems accounting for a substantial share of installations in the north.
Battery storage capacity approaches 20 GWh
Italy’s cumulative connected battery energy storage capacity reached 19.98 GWh and 8.34 GW at the end of September 2026, according to Italia Solare.
The country had 984,829 connected storage systems at the end of the reporting period. Of the cumulative energy storage capacity, 12.55 GWh was associated with PV installations, while 7.37 GWh came from stand-alone storage systems.
In the first nine months of 2026, Italy added 1.95 GWh of storage capacity and 907 MW of storage power across 98,197 new systems. Almost all new installations by number were paired with PV systems. The segment accounted for 98,186 installations, with 1.49 GWh of capacity and 773 MW of power.
The stand-alone segment recorded just 11 new installations, but these contributed 467 MWh of capacity and 134 MW of power.
In the third quarter, PV-coupled storage installations totaled 480 MWh and 252 MW across 31,039 systems. Compared with the second quarter, connected storage capacity declined by 5%, power decreased by 10%, and the number of installations fell by 6%.
However, PV-coupled storage capacity increased by 15% compared with the third quarter of 2025, when 417 MWh was connected. The number of installations declined from 32,697 to 31,039, a decrease of approximately 5%.
In the first nine months of 2026, storage systems associated with PV installations of up to 6 kW accounted for 481 MWh of new capacity. Systems paired with PV installations between 6 kW and 20 kW contributed 596 MWh, while those associated with PV installations larger than 20 kW accounted for 409 MWh.

title: Mozambique entrusts small solar panel factory to UAE's Jampur Group - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
UAE-based Jampur Group has been selected to manage and modernize Mozambique’s Beluluane Solar Panel Factory, which suspended production around 2022 due to technological limitations and market competition. The initiative aims to revive domestic solar panel manufacturing, improve competitiveness and create local employment opportunities.
Emiliano Bellini
24 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
United Arab Emirates-based Jampur Group has been selected to take over the management and modernization of the Beluluane Solar Panel Factory, located in Boane district, in Mozambique’s Maputo province.
The agreement follows a restructuring initiative launched by the country’s Energy Fund (FUNAE) in 2024, aimed at improving the facility’s operational efficiency, addressing technological limitations and strengthening its competitiveness in domestic and regional markets.
Maputo provincial governor Manuel Tule urged Jampur Group to prioritize the recruitment of young people from surrounding communities. However, he acknowledged that the introduction of advanced manufacturing technologies would require specialized skills that may not yet be widely available among local jobseekers.
The factory was inaugurated in November 2013 following an investment of approximately $13 million, financed through Indian cooperation, and had an initial annual production capacity of 5 MW. As Mozambique’s first solar panel assembly plant, it was established to supply equipment for rural electrification projects, including those serving villages, schools and healthcare facilities.
Production was suspended around 2022 as the facility struggled to compete with cheaper imported solar panels and rapidly advancing technologies. Its outdated equipment limited production to panels rated at approximately 270 W, while newer products available on the market offered significantly higher power outputs, further undermining the factory’s competitiveness.
According to figures from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), Mozambique’s cumulative installed solar capacity stood at 175 MW at the end of 2025, unchanged from the previous year.

title: 'When it is your turn, open the door for the woman coming next' - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week, Women in Solar+ Europe gives voice to Italian independent renewable energy consultant Giulia Muia. She says a resilient energy sector depends not only on diversified energy sources but also on diverse voices, perspectives, and inclusive leadership that drive innovation and better decisions.
Empowering women, listening to different experiences, and creating space for emerging talent are essential to building a stronger, more sustainable renewable energy future.
Women in Solar+ Europe
24 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Giulia Muia
Energy is no longer a topic for insiders. It sits in household bills, in the news and in geopolitical choices. It has become a strategic asset and a matter of security. If the energy crisis taught us anything, it is that no one builds security on a single source: diversification is what makes a system resilient. I believe the same applies to the teams building that system.
Gender diversity and inclusion are part of that resilience. With the sector growing so quickly, we have a rare chance to build an inclusive culture now, instead of having to correct it later. The decisions we make about whose voices we hear will shape how the sector grows.
Different people ask different questions
Innovation often starts with asking a different question, and different people ask different questions. In my work, I connect foreign investors, developers, EPC contractors and local landowners. Each of them sees a risk the others miss. Bringing those perspectives together helps us understand a project beyond any single area of expertise.
I have seen engineers and geologists complete every study, only for a local farmer to tell them that the land floods. That single remark can save a project. For me, this is a practical example of why listening matters. The person who holds a crucial piece of information may not be the person leading the meeting or preparing the report. A sector that wants to grow fast, and be accepted by the territories that host it, cannot afford to listen to only one kind of voice.
Creating space, and leaving it
As a leader, I try to make room for different contributions through practical choices. I ask the most junior people first, before senior voices set the direction. I give more time to those speaking in a language that is not their own: I know from experience how easily a good idea gets lost in translation.
I also commit to giving everyone real responsibility, with as little micromanagement as possible. That means establishing clear areas where mistakes are expected and allowed, so we can learn from them without putting the company at risk.
Giving responsibility requires leaving enough room for someone else to use it. Inclusion does not happen by itself: whoever leads has to create the space and leave it.
Learning to take space
Early in my career, as a junior strategy consultant, the head of the company would sit down with me one-to-one, open his notebook and ask: “How can we improve? What has your experience been?” Then he wrote down my answers.
He probably knew it all already, but in that moment I felt I could tip the scales. My experience was worth asking about, and my answers were worth recording. I started preparing, choosing my thoughts and owning my mistakes. Being listened to changed how I approached those conversations and the responsibility I felt for my contribution.
That confidence taught me to take space and, later, as a team leader, to give it. It remains a reference point for how I want to lead: listening to someone can help them recognise the value of their own voice.
Open the door for the woman coming next
My advice to a young woman entering solar and renewable energy is simple: do not wait to feel fully ready. This sector needs more than engineers. I came from M&A and strategy consulting, and that different angle became my strength. Your experience can give you a perspective that others in the room do not have.
Prepare well, then take your space in the room, even when yours is the only different voice. Go to the field. Some of the best lessons come from a landowner, not a report. Look for leaders who listen and invest in you.
And when it is your turn, open the door for the woman coming next.
Giulia Muia is a Renewable Energy Consultant and Strategic Advisor in Italy, providing independent advisory and origination services to industrial groups and utility-scale developers in PV, agrivoltaic and BESS. She connects international investors and IPPs with developers, EPC contractors and landowners, and helps energy-intensive companies through the energy transition. During more than ten years in Munich, she was Head of Business Development South Europe at ZE Energy, International Finance & Investment Manager at Sungrow and Investment Manager at Goodyields Capital. She holds a Master’s degree from the Technical University of Munich, speaks four languages and advocates for inclusive leadership.

title: Glass-free European photovoltaic modules for vehicles, noise barriers and boats - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A European research consortium is developing glass-free photovoltaic modules using fiber-reinforced polymer composites. The technology could enable lighter solar modules for curved and complex surfaces, including vehicles, ships and infrastructure. The project aims to demonstrate industrial feasibility by May 2029.
Marie Beyer
24 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Residential
The European Sunrise consortium is working to eliminate the need for glass in certain photovoltaic applications by integrating solar cells directly into fiber-reinforced polymer composites. The approach could make it possible to manufacture lightweight modules that conform to curved or irregular surfaces, expanding the range of applications for integrated photovoltaics.
“The Sunrise project builds on work already validated by several partners before its launch,” Damien Gautier of the Becquerel Institute, who coordinates two of the project’s work packages, and project coordinator Jaime Cuartero told
pv magazine
The consortium brings together expertise in composite processing, particularly lamination and liquid composite molding (LCM), as well as previous experience integrating polycrystalline silicon cells into composite structures. The partners have also developed laser cutting, texturing and replication techniques to produce multifunctional surfaces. Laboratory and outdoor tests of these surfaces have demonstrated reductions in total reflection of up to 50%.
Building on these results, the project will focus on improving cell cutting, reversible electrical interconnections, molding and lamination processes, while developing encapsulants that facilitate module disassembly, repair and recycling. The consortium has already established the responsibilities of each partner and identified the materials and manufacturing processes to be developed.
Spain’s Aimen is leading research into laser cutting, texturing and LCM processes, while Germany’s Fraunhofer ISE is responsible for developing lamination techniques. Sweden’s Sticky Solar Power will develop a prototype string-manufacturing system using ribbon-deposition technology, which will subsequently be tested by Italy’s Solbian.
“At this stage, the work is primarily focused on the development and validation of these various processes,” the researchers said. They added that a roadmap for scaling up production and industrial deployment will be prepared later in the project, with equipment and manufacturing processes adapted to the facilities of the industrial partners.
Three industrial demonstrators
The project officially began with a kick-off meeting on June 25-26 and is scheduled to run for 36 months, until May 2029. Alongside the development of the manufacturing technologies, the consortium intends to establish an industrial platform for producing glass-free modules and demonstrate their performance through full-scale prototypes tested under conditions representative of commercial applications.
To support this transition from research to industrial production, the partners will adapt the composite manufacturing processes to existing facilities. Lamination developments will be implemented at Solbian and Solitek, while Forster System-Montage-Technik will focus on LCM processes. AIMEN will carry out the laser-related developments and supply the resulting materials to the industrial partners.
Meanwhile, the prototype string-manufacturing system developed by Sticky Solar Power is intended to be installed at Solbian, where it will be used to produce strings for the other demonstrators. Rather than concentrating the entire manufacturing chain at a single site, the project will distribute the processes across three pilot facilities, each specializing in a different stage of production.
“The project will thus rely on three pilot facilities, each dedicated to a specific portion of the developed processes, meaning no single facility covers the entire process chain,” the researchers explained.
The consortium has identified three applications in which the potential advantages of glass-free modules could be particularly significant. The first focuses on vehicle-integrated photovoltaics (VIPV), where reducing module weight is essential for limiting the additional load associated with solar integration. For this demonstrator, the partners aim to achieve a weight reduction of at least 80%, lower system-related costs by 30% and reduce lamination time by at least 50%.
The second demonstrator will target photovoltaic noise barriers, combining electricity generation with roadside infrastructure. In this application, the consortium aims to reduce module weight by at least 30% while achieving 98% of the efficiency of a reference tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) module. The modules will also be designed to withstand a static pressure of 5,400 Pa, addressing the mechanical requirements of infrastructure installations.
The third demonstrator will focus on maritime applications, particularly the integration of PV modules into ship decks. The objective is to develop a continuous solar surface without gaps between individual elements, while incorporating anti-slip properties suitable for use on board vessels. The consortium is also targeting a cost reduction of more than 20% compared with conventional solutions.
Across the three applications, the research aims to demonstrate how composite-based modules could overcome some of the weight and geometric limitations of conventional glass-based PV products. The broader objective is to enable European manufacturing of lightweight, mechanically robust modules that can be integrated into vehicles, vessels and infrastructure without compromising their intended functionality.
The project will also address end-of-life considerations from the design stage, with particular attention to disassembly, repairability and recycling, while ensuring that the resulting products comply with applicable standards.
Sunrise brings together 12 partners from eight European countries, including research institutions, industrial manufacturers and consulting organizations. The consortium covers the value chain from materials development and manufacturing processes to integrated PV applications, while an industrial advisory board will help assess the commercial relevance of the technologies and support their potential deployment.
Challenges for European manufacturing
However, scaling up glass-free photovoltaic technology from prototypes to commercial production in Europe will require overcoming several technical and industrial challenges. One of the main hurdles will be ensuring the reliability and reproducibility of cell processing and encapsulation techniques using fiber-reinforced polymers (FRPs) at an industrial scale. The consortium will also need to demonstrate compatibility with high-efficiency cell technologies, including TOPCon, interdigitated back contact (IBC), perovskite and tandem solar cells, while preserving the recyclability benefits of glass-free module designs.
Certification presents another challenge, as existing standards, particularly IEC 61215 and IEC 61730, were originally developed with conventional glass-based modules in mind. The partners will also need to demonstrate the long-term durability of composite structures under outdoor operating conditions and achieve manufacturing costs that are competitive with conventional PV modules using glass front sheets.
Beyond these technical and economic considerations, market acceptance could prove equally important. “Ultimately, the industrialization of these technologies will also depend on their adoption by a photovoltaic industry that remains largely accustomed to conventional, glass-based encapsulation solutions,” Gautier and Cuartero said.

title: Vietnam orders provinces to introduce rooftop solar incentives by December 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Vietnam has instructed provincial and municipal authorities to introduce support policies for residential rooftop solar installations by the end of December 2026, as part of efforts to secure electricity supplies between 2027 and 2030. The government is also pushing for faster deployment of battery energy storage systems, particularly in northern Vietnam.
Vincent Shaw
24 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Rooftop of the Golden Victory Vietnam’s factory solarised by TotalEnergies.
Vietnam’s government has ordered provincial and municipal authorities to introduce support policies for households installing rooftop solar systems for self-consumption by the end of December 2026.
The instruction was issued under Government Office Dispatch No. 10790/VPCP-CN, dated Oct. 22, following a government meeting on electricity supply security and implementation of the revised Power Development Plan VIII (PDP8).
Prime Minister Le Minh Hung called for faster deployment of rooftop PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS) to reduce peak electricity demand and improve local energy self-sufficiency.
Under the directive, the Ministry of Industry and Trade (MOIT) must propose rooftop solar deployment targets for individual provinces and cities by Oct. 30. The proposals must specify installation capacities and commissioning schedules, with a particular focus on northern provinces, where electricity supply constraints remain a concern.
The government said implementation progress would be taken into account when assessing the performance of relevant ministries and local officials.
Provincial People’s Committees must introduce support policies for households investing in self-consumption rooftop PV systems by the end of December 2026, in line with Article 22 of Vietnam’s Electricity Law. MOIT has been tasked with providing guidance and monitoring implementation.
The directive does not establish a nationwide subsidy rate, leaving local authorities to determine specific support mechanisms.
Energy storage is another priority. MOIT, in coordination with the ministries of finance and justice and other relevant agencies, must develop policies and guidance to accelerate BESS deployment by December 2026. The government is particularly encouraging rooftop PV paired with storage at industrial parks and industrial clusters, especially in northern Vietnam.
The latest instructions build on Directive No. 10/CT-TTg, issued in March 2026, which set targets for expanding rooftop solar deployment at households, government offices and commercial facilities, alongside electricity conservation and demand-side management measures.
Vietnam has also eased restrictions on surplus rooftop solar generation. Decree No. 243/2026/ND-CP, which took effect on June 26, raised the standard limit on surplus electricity sales from 20% to 50% of eligible generation. Higher percentages may be negotiated until the end of 2030, subject to local grid capacity and operating conditions.
The rules also allow eligible surplus electricity discharged from batteries charged by rooftop PV systems to be sold to the grid.
According to state-owned utility Vietnam Electricity (EVN), the country had 134,410 rooftop solar installations with a combined capacity of more than 11.45 GW at the end of August 2026.
However, the rollout of local support measures has been slow. MOIT reported in September that only two of Vietnam’s 34 provinces and municipalities, Bac Ninh and Lai Chau, had adopted the required household support policies.
The broader electricity security program also targets annual electricity savings of at least 3%, a reduction in consumption of at least 10% during peak summer months, and a cut in peak system demand of at least 3 GW.

title: Couple travels through 10 African countries in solar-powered motorhome with battery storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A Brazilian couple traveled through 10 African countries in a motorhome equipped with rooftop solar panels, 15.36 kWh of lithium battery storage, and alternator charging. The system powers household appliances and satellite internet, enabling off-grid travel with minimal reliance on external electricity connections.
Alessandra Neris
24 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
A motorhome that traveled through 10 African countries needed to connect to the grid only about three times during a journey lasting approximately one year. This level of energy independence enabled Brazilian couple Alessandro De Franceschi, known as “Alê,” and Maria Eduarda Cardoso, known as “Duda,” to operate two air conditioners, two refrigerators, an electric stove, and satellite internet equipment, even in remote areas without access to conventional electricity infrastructure.
The couple, who document their travels on social media under the name Getoutsidebr, use a system combining rooftop solar panels, lithium batteries, and charging from the vehicle’s alternator while driving. The system features equipment from Victron Energy, supplied with the involvement of Kamell Comércio Global, and illustrates how integrating solar generation, battery storage, and energy management can increase the autonomy of mobile power systems.
According to Alê, the African expedition began in August 2025. The couple traveled through 10 countries in their motorhome and visited four others without the vehicle. The combination of solar power, battery storage, and alternator charging allowed them to maintain their usual electricity consumption without regularly relying on external power connections.
olar power generation and charging on the move
The motorhome’s electrical system relies on two main energy sources. The first is solar power, generated by rooftop photovoltaic modules that supply electricity to onboard appliances and recharge the batteries during the day.
The second source is the vehicle’s alternator. While the motorhome is moving, a Victron Energy Orion DC-DC charger draws power from the vehicle’s electrical system to recharge the lithium batteries.
The combination enables the motorhome to operate in locations without grid access. The batteries store electricity for later use, while monitoring equipment allows the couple to track the state of charge and power supplied by the different sources.
The system powers a range of appliances beyond basic travel necessities, including an electric stove and oven, an air fryer, two refrigerators, two air conditioners, a television, lighting, and Starlink satellite internet equipment. Water can also be heated electrically, although a diesel-powered option is available.
“Today, we’re able to maintain a daily routine very similar to that of a conventional home, even when we’re far from urban infrastructure,” said Alê.
Battery bank and energy management
Imagem: Divulgação
The motorhome’s electrical system includes three Victron Energy lithium batteries, each rated at 25.6 V and 200 Ah. Based on their nominal specifications, the batteries provide a combined storage capacity of approximately 15.36 kWh, before accounting for discharge limits and conversion losses.
Power conversion is handled by a 24 V, 5,000 VA MultiPlus-II inverter. The system also includes a SmartSolar MPPT 100 V/50 A solar charge controller, Orion charging units, a 500 A SmartShunt battery monitor, a Cerbo GX communication and control hub, and a GX Touch 70 display.
The components work together to manage solar generation, battery charging, DC-to-AC power conversion, and system monitoring.
The motorhome’s energy autonomy depends not only on battery capacity but also on solar generation, electricity consumption, and charging conditions. Running air conditioners, electric cooking appliances, and other equipment simultaneously can significantly increase power demand. The system’s performance therefore depends on the integration of energy sources, battery storage, and energy management rather than installed storage capacity alone.
Remote monitoring tracks solar generation
The system allows the couple to monitor battery state of charge and track electricity supplied by the solar panels and the vehicle’s alternator. The information is available through a display inside the motorhome and can also be accessed remotely via a smartphone.
According to Alê, remote monitoring has proved particularly useful when the couple leaves the motorhome parked while traveling to other destinations by plane. It allows them to check the system’s status remotely and identify fluctuations in solar generation, including those caused by shading on the panels.
In off-grid applications, remote monitoring can help users identify changes in electricity generation and battery charge levels, enabling them to adjust consumption and reduce the risk of power shortages.
However, energy autonomy remains dependent on factors such as solar irradiation, shading, parking duration, and onboard electricity demand. During periods of reduced solar generation or high consumption, the amount of energy available for use may decline.
Alê, 41, from the Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul, and Duda, 33, from Espírito Santo, previously lived in São Paulo and worked as lawyers before deciding to travel across the Americas. Their original plan was to drive from Brazil to Ushuaia, in southern Argentina, before continuing north to Alaska.
What began as a road trip eventually became a way of life. The couple has been traveling for nearly seven years and estimates that they have visited around 30 countries. They document their experiences through their Getoutsidebr social media project, which has attracted approximately 500,000 followers.
Their experience highlights the potential of solar power and battery storage for mobile off-grid applications. By combining onboard electricity generation, energy storage, and battery charging while driving, the motorhome reduces its reliance on external power connections and provides greater flexibility when traveling through remote areas.
The couple also announced in September 2026 that they were expecting their first child, Martin, marking a new chapter in their life on the road. Maintaining a reliable electricity supply and managing energy consumption will remain important considerations as they prepare to travel as a family.

title: Australia’s 2.2 GW Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro cost estimate rises again - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Projects & Applications
Australia’s 2.2 GW Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro cost estimate rises again
The principal contractor for Australia’s 2.2 GW Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro storage project has revised the expected cost to AUD 22.5 billion ($15.8 billion) to AUD 25 billion, with commissioning scheduled for 2029.
Ev Foley
24 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Australia
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Australia’s
2.2 GW/350 GWh Snowy 2.0 pumped-storage hydroelectricity project
is now expected to cost between AUD 22.5 billion and AUD 25 billion through to commissioning in 2029, according to an updated cost and schedule estimate from principal contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV).
The project was initially estimated to cost AUD 2 billion when announced in early 2017. That figure was revised to AUD 3.8 billion to AUD 4.5 billion later that year, AUD 6.1 billion in 2018 and AUD 12 billion in 2023.
The update attributes the cost increase largely to FGJV’s underestimation of the delivery scope, including cost and planning underperformance, and the contractor’s failure to meet productivity targets because of construction complexities. It also cites a design revamp involving detailed technical analysis, and external factors such as global cost increases for equipment, services and labor that exceeded the allowances made at a 2023 contract reset.
Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes said the cost increase is disappointing, but that because the project is no longer on a fixed-price contract, it is no longer exposed to the “weight of billions of dollars in claims from the contractor.”
The 2023 contract reset included mechanisms to support FGJV’s cost and program management on the project, which has more than 5,000 workers. These included directing FGJV to set up a project control office, now operational, that uses enhanced data and analytics to drive productivity and identify emerging risks early.
“Like the original Snowy Scheme, which still underpins energy reliability more than 70 years on, Snowy 2.0 is a generational investment in our energy sovereignty and a national asset owned by all Australians,” Barnes said. “Snowy 2.0’s massive,
long-duration storage
will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills.”
Snowy 2.0, regarded as Australia’s largest energy security project, will provide long-duration energy storage equivalent to approximately 26 million home batteries, or enough to power 3 million homes for a week, according to Snowy Hydro.
The project is transitioning from
cavern excavation and machine tunneling
, which are 90% and 65% complete, respectively, to the
physical assembly of the large-scale underground power station
All six reversible turbines have arrived in Australia. They were manufactured by Germany-based Voith Hydro, with bespoke components fabricated at its facility in Shanghai.
The underground powerhouse complex is a network of caverns about 1 km below ground, which Snowy Hydro said is comparable in scale to the Sydney Opera House. It estimates the complex will last 150 years, until 2176.
In the next phase, crews will install inlet valves, spiral casings, high-voltage transformers weighing more than 400 metric tons each and other hydropower components.
