title: U.S. residential solar prices rise 3.2% as third-party ownership gains ground - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Residential solar prices climbed 3.2% in the first half of 2026 as installers adjusted to the expiration of the federal residential solar tax credit. EnergySage’s latest marketplace report highlights a surge in third-party ownership financing, rising installation costs, and shifting equipment market shares as the industry navigates a changing economic landscape.
MaryElizabeth Q. Mooney
24 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Residential
U.S. residential solar prices increased in the first half of 2026 as installers navigated the expiration of the 30% federal residential solar tax credit, rising labor costs, and continued trade pressures, according to the latest Home Electrification Marketplace Report from EnergySage.
The report, which analyzed solar and storage quotes submitted through the EnergySage marketplace between January and June 2026, found that the median quoted residential solar price reached $2.57 per watt, a 3.2% increase from $2.49/W in the second half of 2025.
For a system at the median size of approximately 12 kW, that translates to an upfront cost of $30,712 before incentives. The average estimated payback period increased from 10.1 years to 10.9 years, although EnergySage noted that a methodology change contributed to the increase.
Median quoted residential solar prices rose 3.2% in the first half of 2026 to $2.57/W, while solar-only pricing remained flat from the previous six-month period.
The pricing trends differed between solar-only and solar-plus-storage installations. Solar-only pricing remained flat at $2.62/W compared with the previous six-month period and decreased 1% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the solar portion of solar-plus-storage quotes increased nearly 5% to $2.55/W, excluding the battery cost.
EnergySage attributed the narrowing price gap between solar-only and solar-plus-storage systems partly to increasing labor costs, as combined installations typically require additional installation time and complexity.
Third-party ownership expands following tax credit expiration
One of the most significant developments in the report was the rapid expansion of third-party ownership (TPO) financing, as installers sought alternatives to traditional solar loans and cash purchases following the expiration of the Section 25D residential tax credit at the end of 2025.
The share of installers quoting third-party ownership products through EnergySage climbed from approximately 14% to 41% between January and June 2026.
The share of installers quoting TPO options on EnergySage increased from approximately 14% in January to 41% by the end of June. EnergySage noted that some of the increase reflects the introduction of TPO products to its marketplace in mid-2025.
Unlike directly purchased residential systems, qualifying third-party-owned projects can continue to access federal commercial tax incentives through 2027, providing an alternative financing pathway for homeowners.
Pre-paid power purchase agreements (PPAs) and leases emerged as particularly competitive options. EnergySage found that pre-paid PPAs offered a 57% lower effective cost per kilowatt-hour than cash purchases, while pre-paid leases were 39% lower.
Traditional PPAs also offered a lower cost per kilowatt-hour than solar loans, although cash purchases remained approximately 33% more cost-effective than conventional PPAs over the comparison period. EnergySage cautioned that the long-term savings associated with newer pre-paid TPO offerings have not yet been established.
Financing remains a challenge for the industry. Median quoted solar loan interest rates held steady at 7.5% for the third consecutive reporting period, while median loan terms shortened from 25 to 20 years.
Pre-paid PPAs and leases offered the lowest modeled cost per kilowatt-hour among financing products quoted on EnergySage in the first half of 2026.
In EnergySage’s contractor survey, 49% of respondents expected the share of customers selecting pre-paid leases and PPAs to increase in 2026, while 37% anticipated declining loan usage and 40% expected cash purchases to decline.
Labor costs squeeze installers as pricing becomes more competitive
Despite the overall increase in median solar prices, the gap between the highest and lowest quotes offered to EnergySage shoppers narrowed.
The average spread between the lowest and highest quotes declined from $0.72/W in the second half of 2025 to $0.56/W in the first half of 2026. The average highest quote decreased to $2.94/W, while the average lowest quote increased to $2.38/W.
The findings suggest that installer pricing is becoming more concentrated following the rush to complete installations before the 2025 tax credit deadline.
At the same time, contractors continue to face higher operating costs. Nearly 74% of contractors surveyed reported increases in hourly labor rates over the previous year. Labor represented an average of 22% of total installed system costs, second only to equipment at 36%.
Affordability remains a central concern for the industry. Approximately 70% of contractors identified electricity bill savings as the primary motivation for customers purchasing solar, while 63% cited cost or pricing as the leading driver of lost sales.
Regional pricing differences also remained substantial. Among the ten largest residential solar states examined, Illinois recorded the highest median quoted price at $3.07/W, compared with $2.00/W in Texas, a 53% difference.
Qcells and Hyundai overtake REC in module marketplace share
The report also identified substantial changes in solar equipment preferences as installers responded to supply chain constraints and evolving sourcing requirements.
Qcells and Hyundai each captured 18% of quoted module share on the EnergySage marketplace in the first half of 2026, surpassing REC, which declined to 17%.
After leading EnergySage’s module marketplace for two years, REC fell to third place with a 17% share of quoted panels, down from 43% a year earlier.
Qcells and Hyundai tied for the leading position, each accounting for 18% of quoted modules. Hyundai experienced particularly rapid growth, increasing its share from 4% in the second half of 2025.
SEG Solar also gained ground, reaching a 17% share, while JA Solar and Canadian Solar saw their shares decline.
EnergySage suggested that the increasingly fragmented module market reflects installers’ efforts to diversify suppliers, manage existing inventory, and navigate restrictions involving foreign entities of concern.
The inverter market, by contrast, remained highly concentrated. Enphase increased its share of quoted inverters to 63%, up 11 percentage points from the previous six-month period. Tesla followed with 29%, giving the two manufacturers a combined 92% share of inverter quotes.
Battery interest rises despite higher costs
EnergySage also reported growing homeowner interest in energy storage, although higher prices continued to limit adoption alongside solar.
Storage interest reached 76% among EnergySage solar shoppers, but attachment rates declined to 31%.
Median quoted battery storage prices increased 5% from the previous six-month period to $1,130/kWh, representing a 9% year-over-year increase.
Despite those costs, 76% of EnergySage solar shoppers expressed interest in battery storage, up from 73% in the previous period. However, the share of solar installations quoted with storage fell from 39% to 31%.
Among contractors surveyed, 64% identified price as the primary reason customers did not add storage to their solar systems.
Tesla remained the most frequently quoted battery manufacturer, with a 52% marketplace share, although Enphase increased its share from 20% to 35%.
Installers look beyond solar for growth
As the industry adjusts to changing solar economics, contractors are increasingly pursuing opportunities beyond traditional rooftop installations.
In EnergySage’s contractor survey, 58% of respondents identified expanding into adjacent products and services as a leading growth strategy for the next three years, including EV charging, HVAC services, and electrical upgrades.
The findings point to a residential solar industry increasingly focused on flexible financing, cost management, and broader home electrification services to maintain its competitiveness in a market without the longstanding federal consumer tax credit.
EnergySage’s findings are based on quotes submitted through its online marketplace and its contractor survey, rather than a comprehensive census of U.S. residential solar installations.

title: Chinese EV maker achieves 504-mile range with using new 96kWh battery
content: Chinese EV maker Li Auto’s updated i6 electric SUV covered 504 miles on a single charge during a livestreamed endurance test, exceeding its official Chinese driving-range rating despite carrying four occupants and running the air conditioning throughout the drive. The vehicle completed the test using a 96 kWh battery, with the automaker reporting energy consumption of 11.8 kWh per 62 miles. The result showcases Li Auto’s efforts to improve efficiency through its own battery-pack design, electric drive motors and silicon carbide power electronics, while shifting away from CATL as a battery supplier. However, the test took place entirely on urban roads in mild weather, conditions that favour EV efficiency and do not reflect typical highway driving or winter use.Urban driving helps the i6 exceed its rated rangeLi Auto conducted the test around Lake Tai in China’s Yangtze River Delta, with temperatures ranging from 55°F to 68°F. The SUV carried four occupants, their luggage and an additional 110 pounds of equipment. The company also kept the air conditioning running during the 18-hour drive.The route consisted entirely of urban roads with speed limits between approximately 25 and 50 mph. Those relatively low speeds, combined with mild temperatures, provided favorable conditions for maximizing range. EVs generally consume more energy at sustained highway speeds, while cold weather can reduce battery performance and increase heating demands.During the livestream, the i6 covered 504 miles before its displayed state of charge reached 0%. Li Auto said the vehicle remained operational at that point, suggesting it might have traveled farther, although the company did not establish how much usable range remained, CarNewsChina reported.The result exceeded the i6’s official China Light-Duty Vehicle Test Cycle (CLTC) rating of 485 miles by about 4%. It also surpassed the model’s reported Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP) figure of approximately 398 miles by roughly 27%.Li Auto moves battery development in-houseThe updated i6 marks a shift in Li Auto’s battery strategy, and instead of relying on CATL for its battery cells, the automaker now uses cells supplied by CALB and Sunwoda, which it then integrates into battery packs designed in-house.The company’s CEO Li Xiang attributed the improved range to the company’s battery design, self-developed electric motors and silicon carbide (SiC) power electronics. These components can affect how efficiently energy moves from the battery to the wheels, making the vehicle’s range dependent on more than battery capacity alone.Chinese media reported that the revised battery design allows the i6 to accommodate an additional 3 kWh of cells. It also reported that updated SiC power modules use revised current paths to reduce operating losses and could add around 19 miles of winter driving range.Silicon carbide semiconductors can improve power-conversion efficiency compared with conventional silicon-based components in some applications, helping reduce energy lost as heat. Combined with improvements to the battery pack and electric motors, those gains can contribute to longer driving range without requiring a proportionally larger battery.

title: US defense-backed power-producing microreactor clears safety milestone
content: US-based Antares has cleared a key regulatory hurdle for its first power-generating nuclear microreactor. The US Department of Energy (DOE) has approved the Nuclear Safety Design Agreement for the company’s Mark-1 system.The decision opens the door for construction and testing at Idaho National Laboratory. It also sets the formal safety standards and technical baseline that will govern the plant until it goes live.The green light comes as the Pentagon accelerates efforts to field reliable, portable nuclear power on Earth and in orbit. In September 2026, the US Space Force granted Antares a $161 million Strategic Breakthrough award to build space-qualified reactors. Military planners want persistent electricity for satellites to support high-demand computing and directed-energy equipment in contested orbital zones.Commercial demonstration for deploymentMark-1 serves as the crucial ground-based bridge toward those ambitions. Antares plans to run the reactor at full electrical power for six months during a major testing campaign in 2027. Unlike pure experimental rigs, Mark-1 is designed as a commercially representative plant.The reactor will produce electricity by feeding heat into a specialized nitrogen closed Brayton cycle system. Operating data gathered throughout the test run will directly inform Antares’ first military deliveries. Under the US Army’s Janus program, the company plans to install the first of several operational microreactors at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, starting in 2028.“Mark-1 isn’t a scaled-down, stand-in test rig,” said Jordan Bramble, chief executive and co-founder of Antares. “DOE’s approval of this safety agreement is the gate that lets us move not only from neutrons to electrons, but to customer plants, on schedule.”The company is moving through federal safety reviews at an unusually rapid pace. This marks the second time in twelve months that Antares has entered the energy department’s authorization pipeline.Achieving self-sustaining reactionIts earlier test reactor, Mark-0, took just eight months to move from safety approval to initial criticality on June 4, 2026. That run marked the first time in over 40 years that a privately developed, non-light-water reactor achieved a self-sustaining fission reaction in the United States.Mark-1 borrows heavily from that predecessor. It uses the same full-scale reactor core, high-durability TRISO fuel, and Idaho test bay. However, while Mark-0 focused purely on physics, Mark-1 must prove that the entire electrical generation system can run reliably under sustained operational loads.Alongside Mark-1, Antares is developing the R1-S reactor for orbital flight. That design relies on passive heat pipes rather than mechanical coolant pumps to pull heat from the nuclear core. Fewer moving parts reduce the risk of mechanical breakdowns during long space voyages.Engineers will first evaluate the R1-S on the ground before mounting it to a spacecraft for flight certification. Together, the terrestrial Mark-1 tests and orbital designs reflect a deliberate strategy: prove core reactor physics rapidly on Earth, then scale the technology for defense bases and deep-space missions.

title: 43% more energy in same EV battery size achieved for Chinese Firefly
content: Nio has unveiled its new longer range 60kWh battery variant of its popular Firefly electrical vehicle (EV). This new battery provides the EV with an increased Chinese testing cycle (CLTC) rated range of 348 miles (560 km), up from 261 miles (420 km). All this within a battery pack of the same dimensions, reportedly without increasing the vehicle’s overall weight. This is significant as it appears to offer better performance from a limited space (the battery) without adding weight.The Firefly had an original battery capacity of 42 kWh, meaning the new battery is somewhere close to a 43 percent increase. This is stored energy capacity and doesn’t necessarily translate 100 percent into driving range. In fact, according to reports, the increase in range is somewhere close to around 33%. This is for a variety of reasons, but part of it is due to the battery management system reserving capacity to protect new cells. New battery: same size, more rangeSo, how was this achieved?Designed by Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), the new battery uses something called ternary lithium cells. These cells have an energy density of 187.2 Wh/kg, achieving a high volumetric efficiency of 73.4 percent.While not entirely clear, the second stat here likely relates to how efficiently the cells are packaged inside the pack, rather than its actual volumetric energy density efficiency.If so, this would mean that the cells themselves occupy only some of the available space. The rest comprises things like structural supports, cooling systems, electrical connections, etc. So, CATL has managed to increase capacity by combining higher-energy-density cells with more efficient packaging. In other words, you can get more electricity into the same physical box without making that box heavier.Another important change is the battery chemistry. The original 42 kWh battery used lithium iron phosphate (LFP), whereas the new battery has changed to nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM).Nice to have optionsThe latter benefits from higher energy density but at a cost. Materials are generally more expensive, and cycle life can suffer when compared to LFP. That said, NCM tends to perform better in colder weather. NCM cells are generally more susceptible to thermal runaway, so additional protection is necessary. But Nio says its new pack includes enhanced thermal protection and several technologies intended to reduce long-term degradation.Trade-offs like this aside, the new battery can reportedly be installed in an older Firefly without replacing the vehicle. This kind of modularity allows existing owners to upgrade vehicles and could potentially accommodate further upgrades as battery technology improves..According to reports, Nio is offering both purchasing and rental options for the new battery-carrying Firefly. Customers can purchase it for $20,400 (about 136,800 Yuan), which compares to between $17,900 (119,800 Yuan) and $18,800 (125,800 Yuan) for the older variant.Alternatively, customers can rent the new 60 kWh battery for around $90 (599 Yuan) a month through its “battery-as-a-service” (Baas). For customers wishing to upgrade older Fireflys, costs come in at around $2,500 (17,000 Yuan) for full purchase or a $450 (3,000 Yuan) service fee for BaaS customers.

title: F-110 warship packs four times the capacity with 64 missile launch cells
content: The Spanish Navy is working with Navantia to develop a much more powerful air-defense variant of its new F-110 frigate. These plans will effectively transform the anti-submarine-focused design into a formidable fleet defense platform.The Navy is currently building five F110 Bonifaz-class frigates. These ships are intended to be modern multirole vessels, but they primarily focus on anti-submarine warfare (ASW).The first of the line, the Bonifaz, was launched in September of last year and is expected to be officially commissioned into the Navy by 2028. The last, the Barceló, is expected sometime in 2032.Each ship comes with 16 missile launch cells, a Lockheed Martin SPY-7 radar, an anti-submarine warfare (ASW) helicopter, and other cutting-edge missile defense capabilities.Improving on the F-110The new F-110 IAMD model, on the other hand, will reportedly come with somewhere close to 64 missile launch cells. It will also feature an enhanced radar and “additional aviation flexibility.” The new ship will also be longer, measuring around 16 feet (5 meters) longer than the F-110 at 492 feet (150 meters). It will also measure around 61 feet (18.6 meters) in the beam and have a full-load displacement of around 6,700 tonnes.Arguably the most significant change is the upgrade in vertical launch system (VLS) capacity. Compared to the F-110, the new ship will be capable of carrying around 48 strike-length cells forward of the bridge and 16 tactical-length cells aft for a total of 64.These cells will be capable of carrying a combination of missiles, including longer-range SM-2 missiles and shorter-range Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles (ESSM).An interesting detail is that four ESSMs can fit into one compatible launch cell. So the theoretical maximum is 256 ESSMs rather than 64 missiles, although a practical loadout would probably mix missile types.Summed up, this all provides the ship with significant firepower potential. 64 total cells with a mix of armaments gives it not only pure missile capacity, but also options. Especially if the ship is required to counter a mixture of threats from air, sea, and land.More missiles, many more optionsThis would significantly expand the ship’s ability to protect an entire naval task group, rather than primarily concentrating on defending itself and nearby assets. But this is only part of the equation.The planned improved radar will enable it to deal with a large suite of threats, from low-flying cruise missiles to fast, maneuverable anti-ship threats. Another interesting feature is the planned ship’s so-called “naval combat cloud.” Essentially, this means the ship will form one node in a network of ships that share and coordinate data in real time. This will enable all ships in a fleet to build a shared tactical picture to better coordinate responses to threats.At the time of writing, the new ship is still very much in the planning stages and has not had an official construction contract agreed. The Spanish Navy and Navantia are working from operational requirements, and the final design must still go through procurement.

title: Archimedes' screw inspires molecular motor that boosts current 100 times
content: A machine inspired by an ancient water pump can now operate at the scale of a single molecule. A team of international researchers has built a tiny motor that uses an electric current to drive a screw-shaped molecule into rotation, while the movement itself can increase the current flowing through it by up to 100 times. This discovery establishes a new way to couple mechanical motion and electricity at the smallest scales, opening new possibilities for molecular electronics.Scientists have spent decades trying to build artificial molecular machines inspired by the motors that power movement inside living cells. However, making a molecule rotate predictably under an electric current while maintaining electrical contact with metal electrodes has remained a challenge. The new device demonstrates voltage-controlled rotation with 100 percent directional preference, using a principle that dates back more than 2,000 years. “We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization,” Fabian Pauly, one of the study authors and a professor at the University of Augsburg in Germany, said.The Archimedes screw gets a molecular makeoverThe researchers took inspiration from the Archimedes’ screw, an ancient device with a helical blade inside a cylinder that lifts water (or solids) when rotated. In the new machine, electrons flowing through a similarly twisted structure generate the torque that makes it rotate. Instead of relying on an external mechanical tool to move the molecule, the current itself powers the motion. The motor’s central component is a dithioacetyl-functionalized (13) helicene molecule, synthesized specifically for the study by Michael Pittelkow’s team at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring just a few nanometres, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms. At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Oren Tal and Anil Kumar Singh connected individual molecules between two extremely fine gold tips. These electrodes provided a path for electric current through the molecule. By adjusting the distance between the tips, the team could stretch or compress the molecular structure, changing the voltage at which the current enhancement began.When the researchers applied a voltage, the molecule underwent cyclic motion with a clear directional preference. Reversing the voltage’s polarity reversed the direction of rotation. This gave the team control over the motor’s movement without physically manipulating it.The motion is driven by current-induced forces: as electrons pass through the helical molecule, they transfer angular momentum to it. The molecule’s handedness helps determine the direction of rotation, much as the thread of a conventional screw determines how it advances. The researchers demonstrated that the direction could be switched by reversing the voltage polarity. Other researchers have also developed DNA-based molecular nanomachines, although they use a different source of energy to generate motion.The spinning molecule opens a better path for electronsThe study authors also observed a surprising electrical effect: once the molecule began moving, the current could rise sharply. To understand why, they used quantum-mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.Their calculations showed that the molecule conducts electricity very differently depending on its rotational angle. As it rotates, it can access configurations that allow electrons to flow much more easily, increasing conductance by up to two orders of magnitude, or roughly 100 times. “The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible,” Léon Martin, one of the researchers and a PhD student at the University of Augsburg, said.Next, the researchers developed a simplified model that reproduced the observed rotation and current increase. Their calculations also predict that, above a threshold voltage, the molecule can transition from stepwise movement to continuous rotation. Such calculations are part of a wider effort to understand why molecular simulations remain challenging.“In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. Yuta Ito, one of the study authors, said.A motor, not yet a miniature machine shopThe findings could help researchers develop molecular electronic components, spintronic devices that use electron spin to process information, and tiny systems for manipulating fluids. They also offer a way to investigate how mechanical motion and electrical transport interact at the molecular scale.However, the device remains a laboratory prototype based on an individual molecule held between gold electrodes. Its performance in practical devices has not yet been established, and the proposed applications remain possibilities rather than demonstrated uses. Further research will be needed to determine how the motor behaves under different operating conditions and whether the principle can be incorporated into functional molecular technologies. The study is published in the journal Nature.

title: Tesla's flying Roadster gets fighter jet graphics, thruster data
content: Tesla’s second-generation Roadster pairs ambitious performance hardware with a cockpit interface designed around driving data. Videos from the company’s October event offer a closer look at the touchscreen, revealing how drivers will control the electric sports car’s adjustable aerodynamics and track-focused systems.The display uses a dark interface with red and white graphics, drawing inspiration from fighter jet cockpit screens. Its layout places key vehicle information within easy reach. Smaller displays near the bottom of the windshield also show speed and lap data, helping drivers monitor performance without looking away from the road for long.Production remains scheduled for 2028, leaving time for Tesla to refine the software. However, the footage already offers a detailed look at how the automaker plans to integrate the Roadster’s specialized hardware with its digital controls.A cockpit built for driversThe touchscreen organizes its main functions under five tabs: Home, Vehicle, Listen, Climate, and Navigate. The familiar arrangement should help existing Tesla owners find everyday controls without learning an entirely new interface.Home features a three-dimensional wireframe model of the Roadster. Drivers can zoom into its mechanical components, which appear in metallic gold. The visualization also exposes hardware such as the suspension and thrusters.Inspired by fighter jet cockpits, Roadster’s interface was designed around the pilot pic.twitter.com/xHsyuNVrWo— Tesla (@Tesla) October 23, 2026Touchscreen controls let drivers adjust the rear wing, hood vent, and exterior lighting. The display also provides access to battery information and charging limits. A compact music strip sits above the main navigation bar.The design extends beyond appearance. Tesla has described the interface as distinct from its previous systems, with an emphasis on the Roadster’s specific requirements. A light mode offers an alternative to the predominantly dark presentation, although both retain the same basic layout.Track mode gets technicalThe Vehicle tab gives drivers four profiles: Comfort, Balance, Sport, and Custom. Each offers a different approach to the car’s driving characteristics, while Custom provides more detailed adjustments.Drivers can modify acceleration response, suspension stiffness, and ride height. Additional controls cover aerodynamic components, including the front and rear wings. That flexibility could help owners tailor the car for road driving or track sessions.Track mode takes the interface into more specialized territory. The display presents lap times, session statistics, and a circuit map. It also incorporates vehicle telemetry, giving drivers access to information relevant to monitoring performance on a closed course.The steering yoke adds another layer of control. Its buttons include functions for turn signals, boost, and the drag reduction system, reducing the need to navigate touchscreen menus during demanding driving.Tesla has also shown a thruster pressure gauge reading 5,500 PSI, alongside a boost-readiness indicator. The display connects the Roadster’s unusual propulsion hardware with the same digital environment used for conventional vehicle settings.Everyday controls get personalityThe remaining tabs focus on routine functions. Listen displays album artwork and playback information, while Climate illustrates cabin airflow and seat temperature. Navigate provides the car’s mapping interface.Tesla has also included a playful detail in the reversing view. An animated hedgehog appears to walk up a driveway before waving at the driver. The small Easter egg adds personality to an interface otherwise dominated by performance data.The production version could still differ from the car shown at the event. Tesla has until its planned 2028 production start to adjust the layout and functionality.

title: US Army advances ramjet interceptor for longer-range drone defense
content: L3Harris Technologies is developing a longer-range missile interceptor that could help the U.S. Army counter drones and other aerial threats without requiring entirely new launch infrastructure. The defense contractor has secured a three-year agreement worth up to $60 million to advance the weapon through flight performance testing.The program targets a growing challenge for military air defenses. Small and medium-sized unmanned aircraft can threaten forces and installations, requiring interceptors that balance engagement range with operational flexibility.Flight testing moves forwardL3Harris has reached the second phase of the Army’s Xtended Range Counter-sUAS Missile program. The project operates under the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation & Missile Center.At this stage, engineers will evaluate flight performance using a fully integrated interceptor. The announcement did not specify when testing would begin or disclose results from previous development work.L3Harris claims its design can deliver greater range and speed than existing systems. It also aims to give military operators more flexibility when responding to aerial threats.Those capabilities could help address a persistent challenge in counter-drone warfare. Defenders must respond to different types of aircraft while managing the cost and availability of defensive missiles. An interceptor that can engage targets at greater distances could expand the area protected by existing air defense units.However, L3Harris has not released the missile’s maximum range, flight speed, or demonstrated interception rate. The Army has also not announced an operational deployment date.Ramjet propulsion extends reachThe interceptor’s propulsion system is central to its proposed performance improvements. L3Harris is pursuing an air-breathing ramjet design intended to improve fuel efficiency and extend engagement distances.Unlike conventional rocket motors, ramjets draw oxygen from the surrounding air to sustain combustion. They generally require the vehicle to reach sufficient speed before producing effective thrust, making their integration into missile designs an engineering challenge.For an interceptor, propulsion efficiency can influence how much energy remains available during an engagement. Greater range could give air defense operators additional time and distance to respond to approaching aircraft.L3Harris is combining its propulsion approach with advanced seeker technology. The seeker helps the interceptor detect and track its intended target during an engagement. The company has not disclosed the specific seeker configuration or guidance architecture planned for the weapon.Scott Alexander, president of Propulsion Systems within L3Harris’ Missile Solutions business, said the design combines propulsion expertise with advanced seeker technology. He described the intended result as a modular, cost-effective interceptor that can use existing launch platforms.Existing platforms simplify integrationCompatibility with current U.S. military platforms forms another part of the development effort. Integrating the interceptor into existing launch infrastructure could reduce the need for extensive equipment changes.That approach could also help the Army evaluate the weapon within established operational architectures. However, L3Harris has not identified the specific launch systems that will support the interceptor.The program also aims to address traditional short-range air defense threats alongside unmanned aircraft. That broader mission could give the Army another option for responding to different aerial targets.The next major milestone will be demonstrating the interceptor’s performance in flight. Test results should help clarify whether its propulsion system and modular design can deliver the range and flexibility L3Harris promises.The $60 million ceiling covers a three-year development effort, but the announcement does not establish a final procurement value. The Army has not disclosed production quantities or a fielding schedule.

title: OpenAI takes frontier training offline after agents breach safeguards
content: OpenAI is keeping its most advanced AI training runs away from the live internet after discovering ways its own models could break out of controlled computing environments. The company now uses an offline web environment where models can practice browsing without directly accessing live websites.The policy follows security tests that exposed weaknesses in OpenAI’s research infrastructure. Advanced AI agents found ways to escape virtual machines and reach external systems. Some even exchanged information across environments designed to keep them isolated.Frontier training moves offlineOpenAI’s offline environment gives models access to indexed web pages and cached content. They can search for information and practice web-based tasks without unrestricted access to the internet.That distinction matters as AI models become more capable of finding software weaknesses. An agent with internet access could exploit a misconfiguration to reach systems beyond its assigned environment. OpenAI wants its security boundaries to hold even when models actively attempt to defeat them.The company plans to maintain its offline training policy until improvements in security and monitoring justify broader access. Its decision reflects concerns that conventional sandboxing may not contain increasingly sophisticated agents.Agents find hidden escape routesOpenAI launched a large-scale red-teaming campaign to test its defenses. Teams of advanced models received infrastructure code and configuration details to help them identify potential attack paths.Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can…— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 23, 2026The experiments consumed hundreds of billions of tokens. Agents uncovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities and flaws in OpenAI’s own configurations.Some models chained vulnerabilities together to escape virtual machines. Others found indirect routes to the internet through internal services that retained limited external connectivity.The agents also demonstrated that isolation can fail without a conventional network connection. In one experiment, models running in separate virtual machines used processor cache timing to exchange synthetic secrets.One agent manipulated cache contents to encode information. Another measured data retrieval times to decode the signal. The technique showed how agents could communicate despite restrictions on network traffic and shared files.OpenAI has since patched affected software and tightened its network controls. It also worked with open-source maintainers to fix vulnerabilities in components used by its research infrastructure.Stronger defenses restore trainingA September 20 incident exposed another weakness when an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver. The flaw gave the model limited access to the live internet during a training run.OpenAI contained the incident but paused training and evaluation of its most capable models. Engineers used the interruption to strengthen security controls and improve systems that automatically stop potentially dangerous runs.Training resumed on October 1, after the company completed further assessments. Its defenses now include virtual machines that isolate computing environments from host systems. Network-level protections provide another barrier if an agent escapes its initial sandbox.OpenAI found fewer vulnerabilities as its red-teaming campaign progressed. However, the company expects future models to discover weaknesses that remain unknown today.It has made large-scale red-teaming a core requirement for assessing future training runs. The company intends to keep testing its defenses as model capabilities advance, rather than assume that today’s security measures will remain sufficient.

title: US uncrewed jet that offers human-machine teaming to enter production
content:
The United States is soon to begin airframe production of its new uncrewed fighter jet. For this, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the world leader in Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS), has announced its partnership with Spirit Defense, a Boeing company.
The aim is to support airframe production of the new FQ-42 Vengeance Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA).
Purpose-built, uncrewed fighter jet, developed with USAF
“We’re excited to be working with Spirit Defense,” said GA-ASI President David R. Alexander. “We’ve established our proven design, development, and
manufacturing
capability for the FQ-42. With Spirit Defense we add capacity, which is exactly the kind of production resilience our U.S. Air Force customer is looking for with its CCA ramp-up. This kind of partnership represents the scalable industrial base the Air Force and the U.S. Department of War are looking for from industry.”
FQ-42 is a purpose-built, uncrewed fighter, developed with USAF as part of ongoing investment in next-generation semi-autonomous combat aircraft. The jet’s modular design enables rapid integration of mission systems and mission autonomy software. GA-ASI’s software architecture, demonstrated through live flight tests on multiple airframes, provides the foundation for human-machine teaming in complex combat scenarios,
according to
a press release.
“We’re proud to bring deep manufacturing expertise and proven capabilities to this important program,” said Keith Schrader, president and CEO of Spirit Defense. “Our team understands the responsibility that comes with supporting critical national defense programs, and we’re ready to deliver for our customer and the warfighter.”
GA-ASI has been the sole manufacturer of its line of UAS — which includes MQ-9A Reaper, MQ-1C Gray Eagle, MQ-20 Avenger, and MQ-9B SkyGuardian/SeaGuardian — since the company’s inception in 1992. For the FQ-42 program, partnering with Spirit Defense is a strength multiplier for the company and the nation, offering manufacturing capacity and industrial depth to scale CCA production faster, while strengthening production resilience, and reducing the risk of single points of failure, as per the release.
The company revealed that around the world, GA-ASI is in discussions with numerous international militaries interested in Gambit Series of modular CCAs. The Gambit Series is a family of uncrewed combat jets, derived from our work on FQ-42, XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, and MQ-20 Avenger, and optimized for roles such as electronic warfare, suppression of enemy air defenses (SEAD), Destruction of Enemy Air Defenses (DEAD) and stand-off precision strike, making it a versatile option for evolving security needs.

title: Aging US paper mills set for AI-driven transformation led by ORNL
content: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) is turning to artificial intelligence, digital manufacturing, and advanced materials science to transform an industry that has changed little in decades.A newly launched national initiative, the Center for Research and Advancement of Forest Product Technologies (CRAFT), will develop next-generation technologies to modernize the country’s pulp, paper, and packaging sector, an industry that supports thousands of manufacturing jobs but still relies on aging mill infrastructure.The initiative is led by DOE’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). The program will bring together multiple national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to improve manufacturing efficiency and help domestic producers remain globally competitive.AI to trace bottlenecksRather than focusing on building new mills, CRAFT aims to extract more value from existing facilities through digital transformation. Researchers will use AI-driven process improvement, complex modeling, automation, and data analysis to identify operational bottlenecks, reduce downtime, improve yields, and cut production costs.“The U.S. pulp and paper industry is critical to thousands of rural communities, like the one where I grew up in Maine, but much of the existing infrastructure is decades old,” said Daniel Coughlin, executive director of CRAFT and a senior research and development staff member at ORNL.The center is funded by the Industrial Technologies Office within DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. It is supported by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Idaho National Laboratory, and the newly established National Laboratory of the Rockies, alongside a network of industrial partners.Next-gen pulpingBeyond digital tools, the research program will tackle some of the industry’s most energy-intensive manufacturing stages, including next-generation pulping, chemical recovery, dewatering, and drying. These processes account for a significant share of production costs and offer opportunities for efficiency gains.Gregg Beckham, senior research fellow and National Laboratory of the Rockies lead for CRAFT, said the initiative will combine molecular-scale modeling with AI-enabled discovery and experimental testing to accelerate the commercialization of new manufacturing technologies.The effort is designed to bridge a long-standing gap amid laboratory research and factory deployment.During its first phase, CRAFT will work directly with manufacturers to identify operational issues and determine which pilot-scale technologies should be tested before commercial rollout. The center also plans to provide companies with access to advanced automation, simulation, and data-analysis capabilities that many traditional mills currently lack.Art Ragauskas, chief technology officer for CRAFT and the University of Tennessee-ORNL Governor’s Chair in Biorefining, said the center will help reduce the technical and financial risks of adopting new technologies, helping promising innovations move faster from research labs to commercial production.Beyond research, CRAFT will serve as a national collaboration hub. It will bring together paper manufacturers, equipment suppliers, downstream customers, and researchers to align technology development in line with industry needs and support workforce development.DOE officials said the initiative is intended to strengthen domestic manufacturing, improve the competitiveness of U.S. forest products, and help sustain high-value industrial jobs in rural communities that have long depended on the pulp and paper sector.

title: Robots power US AI foundry lab's push for faster alloy discovery
content: Imagine walking into a lab where robots are conducting careful experiments. They are assisting researchers in the discovery of metal alloys that can snap back into shape after crumbling, or that can snake through easily into human blood vessels.​This is not a scene from a Steven Spielberg movie or a chapter from an Isaac Asimov novel.​It is indeed going to be a reality at the US’s Texas A&M University. The Department of Materials Science and Engineering of the university has received a $2 million grant to build a first-of-its-kind self-driven research lab, named the Aggie AI Foundry.​Automated system test materialThe facility will be fully automated, equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) brainpower and robotic workers. The computer-controlled arms of the robots are expected to test novel metal alloys by mixing, melting, and testing materials based on directions from an AI brain.​These are expected to take these laborious tasks away from humans, which still take a toll on them, and speed up the discovery and development of new metal alloys beyond current capabilities.​”Dr. Karaman and I, along with our collaborators and students, know what it takes to design materials faster. And we have shown it,” said Raymundo Arróyave, a professor in the department. “But the process can still take a toll on humans.”​The Foundry is a brainchild of Arróyave and Ibrahim Karaman, another materials scientist in the department. By building this lab, they hope to free the students for more creative work.​”You want students to be creative, but imagine they are like line cooks in a big, fancy restaurant. They want to be chefs, and we have them chopping onions and cutting tomatoes. We want to free human brains and hands to conduct more science and write papers that share these discoveries with the world.”​Trained AI brain directs robotsIn the lab, AI training will first take place to enable it to propose ideas for transformative alloys. These training sessions will use physical models, algorithms, and human knowledge built through years of trial and error.​Based on the directions from the AI brain, the robotics will mix, melt, and test the materials for the desired qualities using computer-controlled robotic arms. These arms will function in the assembly line, taking samples from a wall cabinet of elements from the entire periodic table, a statement from the university read.​These automated processes are expected to increase the rate at which metal alloys are developed from months to a week or less.​Researchers noted that, with the current systems available, it wasn’t possible to test materials using only a computer. The work must be done on actual materials, they added.​”The computer can predict some behavior, but there’s no computational tool anywhere in the world that can predict how an alloy is going to behave,” Arróyave said.​But once this lab is up and running, AI can try a trillion possible ways of mixing several dozen elements from the periodic table, a feat yet not achievable for the human brain. While AI can discover hidden correlations between elements, make suggestions, and run the experiments quickly, that could fasten the pace of new alloy discoveries.​”While it’s natural to have questions about AI, it can help scientists explore possibilities and make discoveries at a scale we’ve never seen before,” Arróyave said.​The grant came from the WoodNext Foundation, which manages the philanthropy of tech innovator and Roku CEO and Founder Anthony Wood and his wife Susan.

title: New UFO files detail 1,800 mph black triangle near military sites
content: A black triangular object reportedly hurtled through the sky at 1,800 mph near a sensitive US facility, according to newly released Pentagon records. Two experienced military observers described a silent craft that performed abrupt maneuvers before disappearing.The Defense Department published 28 new records on October 23, bringing its UAP archive to 478 files across seven releases. The collection includes recent military encounters alongside historical reports of unexplained aerial objects. One account describes an unusual encounter that raises questions about the object’s flight characteristics and apparent lack of detectable heat.Mysterious craft defied detectionAccording to a Defense Department memorandum, two senior military observers spotted the object earlier this year. The encounter occurred near a sensitive facility in the western United States, whose location remains redacted in the public document.The witnesses described a matte-black craft resembling a delta-wing aircraft. They estimated its span at nine to 15 feet, with a depth of six feet and a thickness of roughly two feet. Its compact dimensions make the reported performance particularly striking.The seventh tranche of U.S. government UFO records has been released today, October 23.Among the material now available:• A 2026 encounter in which federal agents reported a silent black triangle rising above a ridge before descending into a canyon. The files include visual… pic.twitter.com/k7DB56Dv4M— Tom Thompson🛸 (ＣＯＲＴＥＸ ＺＥＲＯ) (@Cortex_Zero) October 23, 2026The object’s movements were equally unusual. It reportedly climbed around 200 feet, shifted sideways, and then plunged downward before vanishing. The observers also reported that it produced no audible noise or visible exhaust trail.Thermal equipment failed to register a heat signature, according to the document. The object displayed no conventional aircraft lighting either, leaving the witnesses without an obvious explanation for what they observed.The Pentagon included a rendering of the triangular craft in the release. However, officials have not identified the object or established what technology might explain its reported flight characteristics.The account is not the only triangular-object report in the collection. Three separate reports describe black triangles observed above sensitive military sites. The recurring shape adds another detail for researchers examining reports of unexplained objects near restricted locations.Historical sightings join collectionThe latest batch also includes records from earlier decades. A 1953 report describes a metallic, elliptical object spotted in Sweden. Another document recounts an unusual sighting in Saudi Arabia in 1957.Other files cover reported flying saucer sightings around California’s Catalina Island. The collection also features declassified documents concerning alleged paranormal activity at Utah’s Skinwalker Ranch.These accounts span different locations, periods, and reported phenomena. Their inclusion in the archive does not establish a shared explanation. However, the documents give researchers more historical material to examine when comparing witness accounts and identifying recurring descriptions.Pentagon continues disclosure effortThe release follows President Donald Trump’s directive to disclose government records concerning unidentified aerial phenomena, UFOs, and potential extraterrestrial life. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other agency leaders are involved in the effort.The Pentagon is preparing additional records for public release, although officials have not specified when the next batch will appear.The triangular-object report leaves important questions unanswered, including the craft’s propulsion system and the source of its unusual flight behavior. Its reported movements and apparent lack of detectable heat make the encounter particularly difficult to explain using the information currently available.The newly published documents offer no definitive explanation for the sighting or evidence confirming an extraterrestrial origin. They do, however, provide a detailed account of an encounter that investigators have yet to resolve.

title: ​200,000 gallons: AI data center heat could power fresh water production
content: Turning the tables, American technology innovation companies are positioning AI data centers as major water producers rather than water guzzlers.​The companies said that with new forward-osmosis-based desalination plants, data centers can produce up to 200,000 gallons (about 750,000 liters) of clean water a day from brackish groundwater for every megawatt of computing capacity.​To make this a reality, two US-based technology innovation companies, Endeavor and Trevi Systems, announced a partnership Thursday to scale up heat-driven desalination plants, with the first pilot deployment at Endeavor’s data center.​Waterless cooling systemThey plan to use the heat generated by AI data centers to power a process that makes fresh water from brackish or produced water, reducing the need for additional electricity to drive the process.​This technology works like a smart water-cleaning machine that uses heat instead of a lot of extra electricity or fresh water. It uses a closed-loop, waterless cooling system, which means it doesn’t need to keep adding new water.​The heat it creates is used for Trevi’s forward osmosis, where water is pulled through a special membrane by a draw solution, much like water being gently sucked through a filter.​Unlike reverse osmosis, it does not require very high pressure. Then the draw solution is regenerated with 60 to 80°C heat so it can be used over and over. This system removes salt and other contaminants while turning the brine into solids, using almost all waste heat.​The system can make up to 31 liters of clean water for every 1 kWh of computing, the company said. That means a 100-megawatt campus could also function like a 20-million-gallon-a-day water plant, with the energy already coming from the computers beside it.​Turning brine into solidsBeyond producing fresh water, the technology also helps avoid a major bottleneck in typical desalination plants. For every liter of freshwater produced, a typical seawater desalination plant sends about a liter and a half of salty brine back to the sea.Treating this salty wastewater is expensive and energy-intensive, so much of it is usually discarded because processing the brine at concentrators costs too much.Unlike conventional desalination plants, which consume nearly 16 to 26 kWh/m³ at their concentrators and 52 to 70 at their crystallizers, Trevi’s system could reduce energy demand by 85 percent.This is made possible by the system’s zero-liquid-discharge technology, which evaporates the brine into solid salt and reduces the need to handle liquid waste.“Every day the world pumps more than a hundred million cubic meters of brine back into the sea. Trevi’s process runs on heat that is normally thrown away, and that changes the arithmetic,” said Jakob Carnemark, founder and CEO of Endeavor.​According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centers consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024. That figure is projected to more than double and rise to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030.​If the heat from that future data center fleet is captured and reused this way, it could theoretically generate “more than half the 130 million cubic meters per day of clean water currently produced by every desalination plant on Earth,” the statement read.​

title: Hypersonic, rocket motor production gets $21.2 million in US funding
content: Albany Engineered Composites has invested more than $36 million in manufacturing capabilities for hypersonic vehicles, solid rocket motors, and space systems, as the company expands production infrastructure for advanced high-temperature materials.The company announced the expansion through AEC Advanced Programs (AEC-AP), a wholly owned subsidiary established in 2021. Its approximately 70,000-square-foot facility in Rochester, New Hampshire, is designed to support the production of advanced composite hardware for extreme operating environments.The investment is complemented by a $21.2 million US government contract awarded in September under the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment (IBAS) program. The 30-month contract will support development of carbon-carbon composite thermal protection systems for hypersonic vehicles and solid rocket motors.Thermally protected facilitiesHypersonic vehicles and solid rocket motors operate under demanding thermal conditions, requiring materials and structures that can withstand intense heat. Carbon-carbon composites are designed for high-temperature applications and can be used in thermal protection systems that help shield critical hardware.Albany said its new facility will support vertically integrated manufacturing, bringing multiple stages of production and development together. Its capabilities are intended to cover advanced composite thermal protection systems and other hardware for hypersonic, rocket motor, and space applications.The Rochester facility includes dedicated equipment for full-scale hardware production. Planned additions in densification, machining, and inspection are expected to expand its capabilities as customer requirements and production volumes grow.The company is also leveraging its near-net-shape 3D-woven composite technology, along with design and simulation capabilities. Near-net-shape manufacturing aims to produce components close to their final dimensions, potentially reducing the amount of material removal and additional processing required.According to Albany, these capabilities could help move advanced composite designs from development into scalable manufacturing.Scaling hypersonic compositesThe expansion comes alongside a broader push to strengthen the US industrial base for hypersonic systems. The $21.2 million IBAS award will support carbon-carbon composite thermal protection systems for hypersonic vehicles and solid rocket motors.Albany has also announced a teaming agreement with Lockheed Martin to pursue scalable production of next-generation US hypersonic systems, including hypersonic glide body applications.Hypersonic weapons travel at speeds above Mach 5, creating demanding thermal and engineering requirements. For glide vehicles in particular, thermal protection is important because aerodynamic heating can expose vehicle surfaces to extreme temperatures during flight.Manufacturing capacity is another challenge. Advanced composites can require specialized equipment, carefully controlled processes, and extensive inspection. Dedicated facilities could help suppliers prepare for higher production volumes as programs move beyond research and development.Chris Stone, president of Albany Engineered Composites, said the combination of existing investments, the IBAS contract and the Lockheed Martin collaboration would help provide scalable high-temperature composite capabilities for customers and the US industrial base.From advanced materials to productionAEC-AP was established to develop carbon-carbon manufacturing capabilities for high-temperature, extreme-environment applications. Its Rochester location sits adjacent to Albany Engineered Composites’ headquarters and research and development operations.The company said the facility is designed to expand as program requirements evolve. Its planned capabilities suggest an emphasis not only on developing advanced materials but also on manufacturing and inspecting finished components at production scale.As the US advances hypersonic weapons and other high-temperature aerospace systems, the ability to manufacture specialized thermal protection components at scale will remain an important part of turning designs into deployable hardware.

title: 2,000-hour durability boosts organic solar cells to 20.4% efficiency
content: A new molecular locking strategy could help overcome the efficiency, stability, and scalability challenges in organic solar cells (OSCs). Organic solar cells offer lightweight, flexible, carbon-based alternatives to silicon and offer vast potential for commercial use. But the cells’ delicate layers typically degrade quickly under heat and continuous sunlightA team from the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering (NIMTE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) worked to solve this stability issue with a molecular-locking strategy that anchors the delicate solar layers together. In particular, it introduces a specialized intermediate layer that chemically anchors the solar materials to the electrodes. This structure creates strong molecular bonds for better energy efficiency and long-term durability across large-scale panels.“We achieved 20.4% small-area efficiency and 18.8% active-area module efficiency,” the study paper stated. Problem with next-gen solar cellsTo understand the development, you first have to understand why flexible solar cells fail.Organic solar cells (OSCs) harvest sunlight using ultrathin molecular films called self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) laid over transparent electrodes.The connection between the electrode and the organic film is slippery. Under intense heat and continuous light, the chemical bonds slide apart. The layers desorb, and the cell dies.This is a trilemma for solar cell experts: the ultimate balancing act between high efficiency, long-term stability, and commercial scalability. Up until now, optimizing for one usually meant sacrificing the others. To strengthen the troublesome solar cell interface, the NIMTE research team inserted an ultra-thin indium chloride intermediate layer that undergoes a localized reaction upon heating. This process drives out loose chlorine ions, forming a dense matrix of interconnected indium, oxygen, and phosphorus bonds. The resulting chemical network acts as a strong anchor, firmly locking the solar molecules in place rather than leaving them loosely attached.Endurance testingHeating the material triggers a chemical reaction that removes loose chlorine ions and forms strong bonds between indium, oxygen, and phosphorus. This process builds a durable protective network across the surface. The newly formed layer holds the solar cell materials tightly in place, greatly improving overall stability.“The interlayer triggers ligand exchange, forming a robust, multidentate In-O-P coordination network that densely and uniformly anchors SAMs,” the researchers noted in the press release. The strategy immediately improved performance across all key testing metrics. Small lab-scale cells reached an impressive 20.4 percent power conversion efficiency. On the other hand, larger modules with a 15.6 square centimeter area set a record efficiency of 18.8 percent. Interestingly, the devices demonstrated exceptional durability. And retained over 85% of their initial output after 2,000 hours of continuous operation under continuous illumination.“We scaled the technique to large-area modules with an aperture area of 15.6 cm2, reaching a record active-area PCE of 18.8%,” said Prof. LIU Quan, corresponding author of the study.This universal chemical-locking strategy offers a pathway for the commercial future of organic photovoltaics. Overcoming the efficiency, stability, and scalability trilemma might bring flexible solar technology much closer to mass manufacturing. One day, surfaces like skyscraper windows, car roofs, and smartwatch covers could silently generate clean electricity using these tiny chemical locks.The findings were detailed in the journal Joule on October 21.

title: IceCube finds ghost particles with 10 billion times more solar energy
content: A US physicist has recently shed new light on the mysterious particles behind the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, and explained that they could help solve some of the universe’s greatest secrets.George Fuller, a distinguished professor at the University of California San Diego (UC San Diego), worked with Francis Halzen, PhD, on an early study involving the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. The Belgian-American physicist earned this year’s physics Nobel for his work on the project.Now Fuller revealed how they travel across the universe and what makes them so difficult to detect. Approximately 100 billion neutrinos pass through each square centimeter of our bodies every second. Most of them leave no trace. Fuller emphasized the importance of understanding neutrinos. “Halzen’s work, and the work of those he inspired with his vision, was foundational in giving humanity a new window on the universe and on the mysterious and notoriously slippery neutrino,” he added.Detecting ghost particlesThe IceCube is the world’s largest neutrino detector. Positioned in Antarctica, near the US Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, it relies on thousands of light sensors buried in holes drilled through about 0.24 cubic miles (one cubic kilometer) of ice to detect neutrinos. The observatory was developed following Halzen’s vision in the 1990s of building a detector deep beneath Antarctica’s surface. At that depth, fewer air bubbles and impurities would interfere with measurements.But spotting these elusive particles requires extraordinary equipment since they interact so weakly with matter. As a result, the site uses a massive volume of the ice to capture signs of them. The IceCube Neutrino Laboratory at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.Credit: Sven Lidstrom, IceCube / NSFWhen a high-energy neutrino hits the ice, it can release charged particles, which generate faint flashes of blue light known as Cherenkov radiation. These flashes can determine the neutrino’s energy and the direction it traveled from.Still, high-energy cosmic neutrinos are extremely rare. IceCube detects only a few dozen each year. Some have 10 billion times more energy than typical neutrinos produced by the Sun. “One detected by a similar experiment has an energy 200 times higher than that,” Fuller said.Even so, their origins remain unknown. “We don’t really know where that neutrino came from,” Fuller said. “The fact that it got here at all may be saying something profound about the universe.”Secrets of the universeAs elementary particles, neutrinos can’t be broken down into smaller parts. There are three types of neutrons: electron, muon, and tau. As they rarely interact with matter, they can travel enormous distances through space at nearly the speed of light. “Neutrinos are truly ghost-like particles,” Fuller noted. “It’s hard to stop them. It’s hard to catch them. How do we even know they exist or where they are?” At the same time, their unique properties allow them to escape extreme conditions near collapsing stars and black holes.According to Fuller, neutrinos can even travel through light-years of lead without stopping, depending on their energy. Despite being so difficult to detect, these particles are incredibly abundant. Estimates suggest there are around one billion neutrinos for every atom in the cosmos.“In that sense, Halzen really is at the frontier of experimental fundamental particle physics,” the physicist concluded in a press release. New discoveries could reveal more about the Big Bang and the early universe.UC San Diego is also part of the Simons Observatory in Chile’s Atacama Desert, which studies the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe, and could also provide clues about ancient neutrinos.

title: Ceramic cell doubles clean hydrogen output with no extra electricity
content: A team of scientists has found a way to double the production of clean hydrogen from steam without using any extra electricity. The breakthrough could help heavy industries cut their reliance on fossil fuels.Most industrial hydrogen today is stripped from natural gas, a process that releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. Chemical plants need vast quantities of this gas to manufacture fertilizers, refine fuels, and make everyday plastics.Now, chemical engineers at the University of Groningen have developed a durable ceramic electrolyzer that extracts hydrogen directly from water vapor. The system runs reliably at the high working temperatures already found inside chemical factories.Details of the research were published in the journal Energy and Environmental Science.Using steam instead of liquid waterSplitting water with electricity is a well-established technology. Standard liquid electrolyzers run a current through water to divide it into hydrogen and oxygen. However, heating liquid water and powering that split demands huge amounts of electrical energy.Protonic Ceramic Electrolyzer Cells (PCECs) address this issue by using steam instead of liquid water. These systems, which operate at intermediate heat between 400°C and 650°C, need significantly less electricity to break chemical bonds. Inside a PCEC, steam is split into oxygen and positively charged hydrogen ions, or protons.“In the PCEC, there is a ceramic membrane, and only the hydrogen without an electron (H+) is small enough to pass through the pores of this membrane, attracted by a negative charge on the other side that allows it to form hydrogen (H2) again,” explained the researchers.“Because the other atoms do not fit through the membrane, the produced hydrogen is kept separate from the rest.” This removes the need for costly purification stages later on.The main bottleneck has always been finding an electrode material that can survive these hot, corrosive conditions while driving the chemical split quickly.Designing a self-assembling electrodeLead researcher Dr. Vassilis Kyriakou and his team solved this by designing a self-assembling electrode based on a perovskite oxide matrix. When the material was heated in ambient air, ions moved across the boundary between the electrode and the membrane. This movement caused tiny praseodymium oxide nanoparticles to sprout across the surface on their own.“We discovered a previously overlooked synergy between membrane and electrode materials,” Dr. Kyriakou concluded. “Our research initially had a different direction, but our first findings made us think of a completely new path. It felt like falling down a rabbit hole, but there was a wonderland waiting on the other side.”To boost performance further, the team treated the surface with an acid wash. This multiplied the number of active catalyst sites across the material.The modified cell ran continuously for more than 500 hours with no drop in stability. It converted more than 95 percent of the electric current directly into hydrogen, while doubling the production rate of earlier designs. The design offers chemical manufacturers a realistic way to run clean “Power-to-X” processes using factory waste heat.

title: Parts of world's most powerful jet engine to be built at expanded site
content: A Connecticut-based company is expanding one of its plants to boost the production of the world’s most powerful jet engine’s components. Pratt & Whitney, an RTX business, announced the start of construction on a new $100 million facility to increase production of F-35 engine components.The expanded site is expected to become operational in 2028, creating more than 120 jobs.Manufacturing of critical rotating jet engine components“Six months ago, we were talking about this investment as a plan and an opportunity to strengthen Poland’s position as a strategic center of excellence for Pratt & Whitney,” said Piotr Owsicki, general manager, Pratt & Whitney in Rzeszów. “Today, we begin turning that plan into reality. Through strong collaboration across our teams and our shared commitment to delivering for our customers, we are breaking ground on a new Rzeszów facility that will expand our ability to develop highly advanced capabilities and technologies.”The new facility will introduce manufacturing of critical rotating components and meet the growing global demand for commercial and military engines, including the Pratt & Whitney GTF, F135 and F100 engines. The expanded site is expected to become operational in 2028, creating more than 120 jobs.Rzeszów site provides advanced manufacturing, technology development capabilitiesThe company revealed that the Rzeszów site provides advanced manufacturing and technology development capabilities for commercial and military engines, turboprops and auxiliary power units. Its work includes the producing critical engine components such as the GTF fan drive gear system, F100 static structures and key F135 parts. The site also manufactures engines for helicopters, business jets and general aviation aircraft — specifically those from the PT6, PW200, PW500/600 and PW800 families.“Six months ago, we were talking about this investment as a plan and an opportunity to strengthen Poland’s position as a strategic center of excellence for Pratt & Whitney,” said Piotr Owsicki, general manager, Pratt & Whitney in Rzeszów. “Today, we begin turning that plan into reality. Through strong collaboration across our teams and our shared commitment to delivering for our customers, we are breaking ground on a new Rzeszów facility that will expand our ability to develop highly advanced capabilities and technologies.”Expansion follows and supports a $200 million investmentThe expansion follows and supports a $200 million investment announced in February for a seventh isothermal forging press at Pratt & Whitney’s Columbus Forge facility in Georgia, United States. These capital projects, expected to be fully operational by 2028, will enable a 30% increase in output of critical engine parts, such as rotating compressors and turbine disks, as per the release.The company also highlighted that Poland represents RTX’s largest investment and employee base outside the United States, with more than 9,500 employees across its Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Raytheon businesses in-country.

title: 310,000-ton LNG supertanker stretches 1,114 feet, targets 30% less CO2
content: Japan has just delivered a giant liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker that could cut nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions by up to 85 percent and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions by 30 percent.Named Tsurugidake, the massive vessel was built by Tokyo-based Kawasaki Heavy Industries and delivered to Sequoia Navigation Inc. at a shipyard in Dalian, China on October 14, 2026. It is 1,114 feet (339.5 meters) long and boasts a deadweight capacity of 310,020 tons. On top of that, the tanker measures 197 feet (60 meters) wide and 94.8 feet (28.9 meters) deep, with a molded draft of 69 feet (21 meters).The ship is the fourth LNG-fueled very large crude carrier (VLCC) delivered by the Kawasaki Group. As per the firm, the supertanker was built at the Dalian COSCO KHI Ship Engineering (DACKS) shipyard in China. The shipyard is a joint venture between Kawasaki and China COSCO Shipping Corporation.“This new design greatly reduces wave-making resistance from bow waves during navigation, enabling greater propulsive performance,” Kawasaki officials revealed. A dual-fuel tankerAccording to Kawasaki, the vessel features a dual-fuel engine. It can operate on both liquefied natural gas (LNG), as well as low-sulfur fuel oil. When running on LNG, the engine could reduce carbon dioxide emissions by about 25 percent to 30 percent compared to conventional heavy-oil engines.The company also estimates that NOx emissions can be cut by 85 percent, and sulfur oxide emissions (SOx) can be eliminated entirely. This means transporting crude oil over long distances could become less polluting.The tanker is powered by an electronically controlled, seven-cylinder, two-stroke MAN B&W 7G80ME-C10.5-GI-HPSCR engine. As a result, it can efficiently operate at low speeds. Meanwhile, the ship is also equipped with a large-diameter, high-efficiency propeller to reduce fuel consumption during voyages.Kawasaki pointed out that it complies with Phase 3 of the International Maritime Organization’s Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) requirements. The standards require applicable new ships to reach a 30 percent improvement in design energy efficiency compared with the original baseline.A more efficient hullThe supertanker features a redesigned bow intended to improve its performance at sea. Conventional oil tankers typically feature a bulbous bow extending below the waterline. But the novel vessel has a different shape. “Kawasaki’s new VLCC replaces the conventional bulbous bow with a newly designed bow form that extends the vessel’s length at the waterline,” the company said. With a cargo capacity of 352,151 cubic meters, the ship can travel at about 15.45 knots. It can accommodate up to 37 crew members. Kawasaki has also installed SOx scrubbers on the exhaust outlets of the main engine as well as the onboard power-generation system.These devices are crucial because they remove sulfur oxides from exhaust gases. This means that the ship can use fuel oil and still meet the emission limits. They also allow greater fuel flexibility. “By installing this equipment, the cost for fuel oil is expected to be reduced since the conventional fuel oil will still be compatible after the regulation reinforcement,” the company concluded in a press release.
