title: Scientists Find That Cats and Their Owners Share a Surprising Biological Connection
content:
A small month-long study suggests that the emotional benefits of living with a cat may depend less on how long the relationship has lasted than on everyday interactions. Credit: Shutterstock
The comfort you find in a cat’s company may have less to do with years together than with everyday closeness, a small observational study suggests.
Cat owners often credit their pets with making life better, but research has produced mixed evidence about whether owning a cat benefits human health and well-being. Some studies have found positive effects, while others have reported possible negative ones.
Researchers at
Kyoto University
wondered whether those differences might reflect the quality of the relationship between people and their cats, particularly their everyday interactions. To investigate, the team followed the daily lives of 29 cats and their 19 owners for one month, recruiting participants through flyers and social media. They assessed owners’ moods through questionnaires and observed how the cats behaved toward their owners and unfamiliar people.
To measure everyday physical closeness, the researchers attached small Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons to the cats’ collars. Owners who spent more time physically close to their cats tended to report more positive feelings. How long they had owned their cats, however, was not associated with those positive mood states. The distinction suggests that daily contact may matter more to this aspect of owners’ well-being than the length of the relationship.
Cats joined our study with the BLE beacon. Credit: KyotoU / Saho Takagi
Cats’ oxytocin linked to owners’ negative moods
Urine samples from both cats and owners revealed connections involving oxytocin, a hormone associated with social relationships, and cortisol, a hormone associated with stress. Higher oxytocin concentrations in cats’ urine were associated with higher oxytocin concentrations in their owners’ urine. Cats with higher oxytocin levels also tended to have owners with lower cortisol levels and fewer negative feelings. The cats’ oxytocin levels were more closely associated with their owners’ negative mood states than the owners’ own oxytocin levels were.
“I think many cat owners are familiar with the sense of comfort and peace they feel when their cat climbs onto their lap seeking affection, they start to pet it, and the cat begins purring contentedly,” says corresponding author Saho Takagi. “Our findings suggest that this feeling may be partly reflected in the hormonal connection between cats and their owners, particularly through oxytocin, a hormone involved in the formation of parent-child bonds and social relationships.”
The findings offer a possible explanation for the inconsistent evidence about cat ownership and health. Benefits or drawbacks may depend on the relationship between a person and their cat, rather than ownership alone. However, the study establishes associations, not cause and effect. The team hopes to explore more deeply how cats and humans influence each other through their everyday interactions.
Reference: “Cats and humans show correlated affiliative physiological states” by Saho Takagi, Taisuke Tsubomura, Miho Nagasawa and Takefumi Kikusui, 13 October 2026,
iScience
DOI: 10.1016/j.isci.2026.117934
This work was supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Research Fellowship for Young Scientists (grant no 22KJ2970) and a Grant-in-Aid for Transformative Research Areas (A) (grant no 26A102), both awarded to S.T., by the Ayako Ueda Fund Research Grant Program of the Japanese Society of Feline Medicine, and by the Hakubi Project at Kyoto University.

title: New Research Reveals Cows Have a Little-Known Ability To Recognize Humans
content:
New research suggests cows possess a surprisingly sophisticated ability to recognize humans using multiple senses. Credit: Shutterstock
A stranger’s face can hold a cow’s attention longer than a familiar handler’s, video tests suggest, offering clues to how cattle recognize the people around them.
When cows watched videos of people, they looked longer when the face on screen matched the voice they heard. The finding suggests that these highly social animals, which live in close contact with humans, can connect a person’s appearance with their voice.
Océane Amichaud of INRAE in Nouzilly, France, and colleagues tested these abilities in 32 Prim’ Holstein cows (
Bos taurus taurus
). Their study, published in the open-access journal
PLOS One
, examined both how the animals responded to human faces and whether they could link information from sight and hearing.
Cows distinguish faces and match voices
In the visual tests, the researchers played muted videos of familiar and unfamiliar male faces and measured how long the cows watched them. Unfamiliar faces held the animals’ gaze longer than a familiar handler’s face. That preference for new faces indicated that the cows could distinguish between people they knew and people they did not.
Experimental setup for visual preference and cross-modal tests. The cow was positioned centrally between two screens. Each screen showed a video of a person’s face: one familiar and one unfamiliar to the cow. During cross-modal tests, a speaker placed between the screens played the voice of one of the two individuals. Cameras recorded the cow’s behavioral responses throughout the test. Credit: Amichaud et al., 2026, PLOS One,
CC-BY 4.0
The researchers also tested cross-modal recognition, the ability to connect information received through different senses. They showed videos of familiar and unfamiliar faces while playing a recording of one of the two men speaking. Each man said the same sentence, keeping the words consistent across the recordings.
“In this study, using visual preference and cross-modal tests, we showed that cows are able to process human faces presented in 2D on videos and to associate familiar and unfamiliar faces with the corresponding voices by integrating multiple sensory modalities,” the authors said.
Recognition without detectable emotional change
Heart rate measurements taken while the cows watched the videos did not reveal evidence that familiar or unfamiliar faces and voices affected their emotional responses. Differences in how long the animals looked therefore did not correspond to an emotional change detectable through this measure.
The authors caution that watching a video and hearing a recording are not equivalent to interacting with a person. Although the results suggest that cows can identify people through their faces and voices, further studies could examine how the animals interact with specific individuals. Understanding those relationships could help guide efforts to support their welfare.
Reference: “Cows visually discriminate and cross-modally recognise familiar and unfamiliar human faces in videos” by Océane Amichaud, Julie Lemarchand, Fabien Cornilleau, Plotine Jardat, Vitor H. B. Ferreira, Ludovic Calandreau and Léa Lansade, 20 May 2026,
PLOS ONE
DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0329529
This study was funded by the French National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and the Environment. The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

title: These Giant-Headed Ants Are Breaking a Fundamental Rule of Biology
content:
Pheidole is one of the most diverse genera of ants, with more than 1,000 described species found across much of the world, particularly in tropical regions. Commonly known as big-headed ants, their colonies typically contain two distinct worker castes: smaller workers that gather food and care for the colony, and larger soldiers with oversized heads and powerful jaws that help defend the nest and process food. Credit: Shutterstock
Bigger animals generally have bigger body parts, but new research reveals that certain ants defy this biological rule.
In the insect world, bigger bodies usually come with bigger body parts. But some ants break this rule in an unexpected way. A massive soldier ant, equipped with an oversized head and powerful jaws, can have smaller antennae than a worker that is only a fraction of its size.
Researchers at the
University of Ottawa
have discovered that this unusual pattern is widespread among
Pheidole
ants, a diverse group known for their distinct worker and soldier castes. Although antennae grow in proportion to body size within each caste, their sizes overlap between castes despite major differences in overall body size.
The findings suggest that evolution can alter how individual body parts grow, allowing ants to develop specialized features without following the usual rules of biological scaling.
A Surprising Discovery Across Hundreds of Ant Species
“It was total serendipity. We were sitting at the microscope and Erica (Erica Vong is a graduate researcher and student at uOttawa and lead author of this study) showed me the antennae of two individuals. One was clearly smaller, yet it turned out to be from the soldier!” says Rajendhran Rajakumar, Associate Professor of Biology at the University of Ottawa.
The smaller antennae belonged to a soldier, while the larger ones came from a worker. “Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae.”
Using laboratory experiments, field data, and museum collections, researchers examined 565
Pheidole
species and found the pattern throughout the genus. Comparisons suggest it may have originated near the common ancestor shared with
Cephalotes
turtle ants.
“Biologists have long assumed that traits such as antennae generally scale predictably with body size,” Professor Rajakumar says. “Our findings show that evolution can decouple a trait from body size in one context while preserving that relationship in another.”
How Ant Colonies Control Body Growth
Antennae allow ants to detect chemical signals, navigate their surroundings, and communicate with nestmates. Their size and shape also influence the arrangement of sensory structures.
“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Professor Rajakumar explains. “In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”
Experiments with
Pheidole dentata
showed that social signals, juvenile hormone, and an organ involved in regulating body proportions influence this flexibility. By manipulating these factors, particularly the soldier inhibitory pheromone, researchers produced unusual “nanoworkers” and “nanosoldiers.” The nanosoldiers had worker-sized bodies but the enlarged heads characteristic of soldiers.
“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” clarifies Professor Rajakumar. “They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”
Breaking Biological Rules Through Evolution
The results demonstrate how colony conditions can influence individual development, supporting the concept of an ant colony as a superorganism. This flexibility may have contributed to the evolution of specialized castes and the remarkable diversity of ants.
“This work reminds us that evolution is not always a process of adding more or less of the same trait,” Professor Rajakumar concludes. “Sometimes new possibilities emerge when the expected connections between traits are broken and development is reorganized.”
Reference: “Breaking trait scaling via the evolution and regulation of dimorphic decoupling in ants” by Erica Vong, Shannon Parisien, Hélène Orfali and Rajendhran Rajakumar, 6 October 2026,
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2612172123

title: Your Saliva Could Hold the Key to Detecting a Deadly Cancer
content:
Although still experimental, a simple saliva test could one day offer a low-cost way to identify patients who need further screening for esophageal cancer. Credit: Stock
Scientists have discovered distinct bacterial patterns in the saliva of patients with a deadly form of esophageal cancer.
Bacteria living in the mouth may hold clues to a deadly form of esophageal cancer that often goes undetected until treatment options are limited. Researchers in South Africa have identified distinctive bacterial patterns in patients’ saliva, raising the possibility that a simple, inexpensive test could eventually help identify people who need further screening.
The study, published in
Communications Medicine
, was conducted by scientists at the Sydney Brenner Institute for Molecular Bioscience (SBIMB) at Wits University and Columbia University in New York. Combining bacterial DNA sequencing with machine learning, the team developed a model that distinguished cancer patients from unaffected individuals more effectively than one based on clinical and demographic information alone.
A Deadly Cancer With Mysterious Geographic Patterns
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is especially common in parts of eastern and southern Africa, including South Africa’s Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces. High rates also occur in regions of China and Iran, forming a geographic belt that scientists have struggled to explain.
Unlike esophageal adenocarcinoma, which is strongly associated with acid reflux, obesity, and lifestyle factors, ESCC has less clearly understood causes. It also frequently affects relatively young adults.
“A feature of the cancer is the young age of many patients, with a mean age of 50, and 18% of patients presenting before the age of 40,” says Distinguished Professor Christopher Mathew of the SBIMB.
“This geographical occurrence is also puzzling, and may reflect genetic susceptibility, a specific environmental exposure, or a combination of factors that researchers have still not been able to pin down,” explains Dr. Wenlong Carl Chen, a researcher at SBIMB.
Known Risk Factors Cannot Explain Every Case
Analysis of data from the
Johannesburg Cancer Study
identified several ESCC risk factors, including smoking, heavy alcohol consumption, rural residence, lower educational attainment, and the use of biomass or other household fuels.
“Still, they do not fully explain the number of cases, the geographic clustering, or why some patients develop the disease without these obvious exposures.”
To investigate another possible indicator, researchers examined the oral microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the mouth. DNA sequencing revealed distinct differences between saliva samples from cancer patients and unaffected controls.
“We found clear differences between the saliva bacteria of people with oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma and unaffected controls. Using genetic sequencing of bacteria and machine-learning methods, the team identified a distinctive microbial pattern associated with the cancer,” says Chen.
Saliva Bacteria May Signal Changes in the Esophagus
Several bacterial species were more abundant in ESCC patients, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, a microorganism previously implicated in other cancers. The microbiome-based model also performed better than one relying solely on clinical and demographic data.
However, the findings do not establish that these bacteria cause cancer. The microbial changes could instead result from the disease itself, particularly as a growing tumor narrows the esophagus and disrupts normal swallowing.
“But even that could be useful. A blockage in the esophagus develops gradually, often before patients arrive at the hospital, unable to swallow properly. If microbial changes in saliva can help flag that something is already changing, they could one day help identify people who need earlier referral for endoscopy.”
A saliva or cheek swab test could eventually help doctors prioritize patients for endoscopy, particularly in communities with limited access to specialized care. Such a test would not replace endoscopy, however, and the current approach has not been established as an early cancer detection method.
Searching for Genetic and Environmental Clues
Researchers are also investigating whether inherited genetic differences increase susceptibility to ESCC and whether tumors contain evidence of earlier environmental exposures.
One approach involves studying mutational signatures, distinctive patterns of DNA damage preserved in cancer cells. Certain chemicals, pollutants, smoke exposures, or water contaminants may leave recognizable genetic traces, potentially helping scientists identify contributors to the disease.
“This is critical research which has generated important foundational knowledge that will take us to the next step, and hopefully to the clinic in the long run,” says Professor Michèle Ramsay, Director of the SBIMB.
What Researchers Need to Confirm
The saliva model has undergone internal validation but still requires testing in independent populations. Oral bacterial communities vary with geography, diet, and environmental conditions, meaning results from one population may not translate directly to another.
The next research phase will include patients with confirmed ESCC, healthy individuals, and people with benign esophageal conditions that can also cause swallowing difficulties.
These comparisons will help establish whether the bacterial patterns are specific to cancer or reflect esophageal obstruction more generally. The answer will determine whether saliva testing could eventually become a practical tool for identifying patients who need further investigation.
Reference: “A generalizable cross-continent prediction of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma using the oral microbiome” by Shahd ElNaggar, Wenlong Carl Chen, Leanne M. Prodehl, Thomas K. Marumo, Muhammed U. Khan, Christopher G. Mathew, Paul Ruff, Zhezhen Jin, Alfred I. Neugut, Anil K. Rustgi, Anne-Catrin Uhlemann, Tal Korem and Julian A. Abrams, 28 February 2026,
Communications Medicine
DOI: 10.1038/s43856-026-01468-y

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Cholesterol Switch That Could Change How We Treat Heart Disease
content:
High cholesterol can quietly weaken the liver’s ability to clear harmful fats from the bloodstream. Scientists have uncovered a hidden biological mechanism behind this process, revealing a promising new direction for cholesterol-lowering treatments. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers uncovered how a high-cholesterol diet weakens the liver’s defenses and lowered LDL in mice by blocking the pathway, pointing to a potential new use for a shelved heart failure drug.
A diet high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the liver’s ability to remove harmful cholesterol from the blood. Cholesterol-related heart disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide, even as doctors have gained more medications to treat it.
Researchers at the
University of California San Diego School of Medicine
have identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why the liver’s cholesterol-clearing capacity declines. Their study, published in
, combined experiments in mice and human cells and identified a potential treatment target. An experimental drug that acts on that target has already undergone initial safety testing in humans, potentially shortening the route to a clinical trial for high cholesterol.
More receptors, more cholesterol cleared
The liver normally removes cholesterol from the blood so it can be broken down and used elsewhere. Proteins called LDL receptors sit on the surface of liver cells, where they capture harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and pull it inside for processing. More receptors mean more cholesterol can be cleared. Most cholesterol-lowering drugs, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, work by increasing or preserving the number of these receptors.
Some patients, however, cannot tolerate the side effects of available medications.
“There’s still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can’t get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now,” said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. “This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap.”
Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. Credit: UC San Diego Health Sciences
Blocking CTSA lowers LDL in mice
The newly identified pathway works against cholesterol removal by gradually depleting LDL receptors. It begins when high dietary cholesterol activates Ral, a protein Saltiel previously studied in fat cells. As Ral activity increases, fewer LDL receptors remain available to pull cholesterol from the bloodstream, contributing to higher blood cholesterol.
That receptor loss ultimately depends on an enzyme called cathepsin A, or CTSA. When the researchers blocked CTSA with a small molecule inhibitor, they stabilized LDL receptors and sharply lowered circulating LDL cholesterol in mice.
“We’ve known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver’s ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn’t fully understand why,” said Saltiel. “This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle.”
A shelved drug could target cholesterol
Turning a biological discovery into a treatment usually requires substantial additional research to find a suitable drug. In this case, a CTSA inhibitor had already been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. It reached a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully tested for safety, before being shelved for strategic reasons.
That earlier work could allow the investigational drug to move into a Phase 2 trial for high cholesterol. The reduction in LDL cholesterol demonstrated in mice has yet to be established in people.
“Luckily, there’s an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that’s already been shown to be safe in humans,” said Saltiel. “We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial — which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected.”
Reference: “Dietary cholesterol activates a Ral-dependent pathway driving LDLR turnover” by Xue Feng, Shuo Zhang, Yuqi Wang, Twisha Kurlagunda, Allyssa Sit, Priyadarshini Jaishankar, Pusu Yang, Sadatsugu Sakane, Se Yong Park, Churaibhon Wisessaowapak, Kaylee Nguyen, Jamie Yan, Himani Pothulu, Catherine Dinh, Felicia Chu, Yuyao Ren, Bichen Zhang, Patrick Secrest, Linmeng Han, Chao-Wei Hung, Preethi Veeragandham, Yuliya Skorobogatko, Tatiana Kisseleva, Philip L.S.M. Gordts, Adam R. Renslo, Peng Zhao, Amit R. Majithia and Alan R. Saltiel, 24 June 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10697-z
This study was funded, in part, by the National Institutes of Health (Grants P30DK063491, R01DK117551, R01DK128796, and R01DK135289) and an American Diabetes Association postdoctoral fellowship (1-25-PDF-76).

title: A Major Drug Breakthrough Could Change How Ozempic and Wegovy Work
content:
Illustration of small molecule modulation of β-arrestins and GPCR signaling pathways based on concepts developed by the Lefkowitz Laboratory, Duke University. Credit: Ella Maru Studio / Duke University
New compounds have overcome a longstanding challenge by directly targeting β-arrestins, proteins that regulate cellular signals, providing laboratory tools that could help guide more precise treatments with fewer side effects.
A drug can hit its intended target and still have its effects cut short. That’s because cells have built-in molecular brakes that dial down signals after a receptor is activated. Now, scientists have discovered a way to interfere with those brakes, keeping an important signaling pathway active longer at the same receptor targeted by the blockbuster weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy.
The breakthrough involves three new drug-like molecules that block β-arrestins, proteins that normally dampen cellular signals. In laboratory experiments, the compounds prolonged signaling without directly targeting the GLP-1 receptor, opening a potential path toward more precise medicines with fewer side effects.
Decades ago,
Duke University
biochemist and cardiologist Robert J. Lefkowitz, MD, and his colleagues discovered those regulatory proteins, called β-arrestins. Now, work from his laboratory, published in
, gives scientists their first chemical tools for directly controlling β-arrestins and investigating how they shape cellular responses.
β-Arrestins restrain some signals and trigger others
β-Arrestins help regulate G protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs, the family that includes the GLP-1 receptor. Nearly every human cell depends on GPCRs to receive and send signals for normal function, and roughly one-third of all FDA-approved drugs target them. When these receptors become active, G proteins relay their signals within the cell. β-Arrestins can limit the response by attaching to the receptors, dampening their signaling, and drawing them inside the cell.
In the early 2000s, the Lefkowitz lab established that β-arrestins also initiate signaling pathways of their own. That discovery revealed two distinct roles for the proteins, restraining signals carried by G proteins while setting other cellular responses in motion. The new compounds let researchers interfere directly with both β-arrestin functions while preserving G protein signaling.
Blocking β-arrestins preserves G protein signaling
Finding and understanding these molecules took more than a decade of work by co-first authors Alem W. Kahsai, PhD, an assistant professor of medicine, and Natalia Pakharukova, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher. Lefkowitz said Kahsai “lived and breathed” the molecules 24 hours a day, bringing together collaborators from Duke and across the country to “describe an extraordinary amount of their biology.”
The search started with a broad, unbiased screen of the National Cancer Institute’s extensive compound library. Researchers looked for molecules that might bind β-arrestins, then used additional tests to establish which candidates physically attached to the protein and stabilized it.
Robert Lefkowitz, MD, Alem Kahsai, PhD, and Natalia Pakharukova, PhD. Credit: Duke University
To see what that binding accomplished, the team tested promising compounds in engineered human cells that allowed GPCR signaling to be monitored as it happened. Experiments then moved into physiologically relevant immune cells and heart muscle cells, allowing the researchers to assess whether the effects held beyond simplified laboratory systems.
Three compounds emerged that prevented β-arrestins from being recruited to receptors. They blocked desensitization, which reduces a receptor’s responsiveness, and internalization, which moves receptors inside the cell. The compounds also suppressed β-arrestin-specific signaling. Tests across several GPCRs showed that G protein signaling remained intact, including at the GLP-1 receptor, where it continued longer than usual even during stimulation with Ozempic and Wegovy.
“We tested these compounds from every angle we could think of before we were convinced they were bona fide β-arrestin inhibitors,” Kahsai said.
Binding to a pocket reshapes β-arrestin
Pakharukova uncovered a structural explanation using cryo-electron microscopy. She visualized a compound called Cmpd-5 nestled in a previously unknown pocket on β-arrestin. Binding there altered the protein’s overall shape, leaving it unable to fully engage with GPCRs. This mechanism is called allosteric inhibition, because a molecule binding at one site changes how the protein functions elsewhere.
“Alem could have published a creditable paper about these molecules 10 years ago,” said Lefkowitz, Duke Health Distinguished Professor of Medicine and the study’s senior author. “But he’s a perfectionist. He wanted to figure out how they actually work.”
The ability to control β-arrestins with pharmacological precision could help researchers determine how individual signaling pathways influence metabolism, immune responses, cardiovascular function, and brain signaling. Eventually, adjusting those pathways could offer a route to more precise treatments with fewer unwanted side effects.
Reference: “Small-molecule modulation of β-arrestins” by Alem W. Kahsai, Natalia Pakharukova, Henry Y. Kwon, Kunal S. Shah, Caroline T. del Real, Bowie N. Shreiber, Jason G. Liang-Lin, Paul J. Shim, Mason A. Lee, Van A. Ngo, Allison M. Schwalb, Uyen Pham, Anand Chundi, Haoran Jiang, Emmanuel Flores-Espinoza, Samuel Liu, Preston C. Nibley, Dana K. Bassford, Hyunggu Hahn, Cal A. Kunzle, Brittany N. Thomas, Jihee Kim, Yang Zhou, Jialu Wang, Xingdong Zhang, Jeffrey S. Smith, Lindsay A. M. Rein, Alex R. B. Thomsen, Sudha K. title: Researchers Find an Unexpected Benefit of Putting Sheep on Solar Farms
content:
A solar farm in Lansing, New York. Credit: Sreang Hok/Cornell University
Solar grazing is helping sheep farmers expand their businesses, opening opportunities for rural jobs, new investment, and stronger agricultural supply chains.
Sheep can feed on the vegetation growing around solar panels while farmers get paid to keep it under control. Too few sheep may leave farmers with grass they still need to mow, while heavier grazing can reduce honeybee numbers.
Cornell University
studies examine the ecological and financial choices behind this growing practice, known as solar grazing. One tested how the number of sheep on the land affects beneficial insects. The other developed a tool to help farmers plan flock size, purchases, and sales.
More sheep, fewer honey bees
At two sheep per hectare, or roughly one per 1.2 acres, the combined abundance of wild bees, honey bees, and lady beetles was 38% higher than in a mowed control plot. Honey bee numbers were 83% higher, accounting for most of the overall increase.
Doubling the density to four sheep per hectare improved vegetation control, but beneficial insect abundance was similar to that in the mowed control. Eight sheep per hectare delivered the strongest vegetation control, and flock health remained high. At that density, however, honey bee abundance fell by 45%.
“We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said Steve Grodsky, the study’s senior author and an assistant professor of natural resources in Cornell’s Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants, and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”
The researchers spent three years testing those stocking rates, the number of sheep grazing a given area, at the university-owned
Cascadilla Community Solar Farm
in Dryden, New York. Using Cornell’s teaching flock, the team brought together entomologists, ecologists, and animal and plant scientists from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). Their paper was published in
Environmental Research Letters
“Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Ashley School. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”
Grodsky also serves as assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Sarah Carson, director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, helped coordinate the researchers’ access to the site with the solar company responsible for managing it.
The study’s other CALS co-authors included sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20, Antonio DiTommaso, a professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science, and John Losey, a professor of entomology. Also contributing were Scott McArt, Ph.D. ’12, an associate professor of entomology, Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab, and Todd Ugine, Ph.D. ’04, a research associate in Losey’s lab.
Planning flock growth around grass and costs
For farmers deciding how many sheep to buy or sell, the second study offers a way to weigh the financial and practical demands together. Researchers led from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business developed a spreadsheet-based model that uses target flock size, costs, anticipated revenue, and expected vegetation at individual solar sites to help optimize those decisions. They presented the tool in a separate study published in
Manufacturing & Service Operations Management
Solar developers can also use the model to understand what farmers need from a grazing agreement and design contracts that are more profitable and sustainable for everyone involved over the long term. United Agrivoltaics has already made the tool part of its onboarding process.
The project grew out of a chance meeting between the paper’s first author, Vincent Slaugh, an assistant professor at the Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and Caleb Scott, an Ithaca-based sheep farmer who founded United Agrivoltaics. Afterward, Slaugh began working through the economics and logistics of grazing sheep at solar installations. He recruited Linwei Xin, an associate professor of operations research and information engineering, and Shane Henderson, the Charles W. Lake, Jr. Professor in Productivity, both in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering.
Solar contracts help sheep farms expand
Kochendoerfer’s solar grazing operation includes 700 ewes at installations in New York and Vermont.
“I work with a lot of farms that are now scaling up because of solar,” Kochendoerfer said. “There is a new wave of sheep farmers who are capitalizing on this access to good land. With solar grazing, you get paid to graze as opposed to having to pay to graze. That leads to sustainable, meaningful economic income that these farmers can use to expand, build a barn, buy equipment or hire someone. It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.”
Slaugh sees the steady income and animal feed available through solar contracts as an opportunity for American shepherds to increase production. U.S. sheep production falls well short of domestic demand for meat and wool. About
half of the lamb and mutton consumed in the United States is imported
, mainly from New Zealand and Australia.
“If we grow the sheep industry, will the American diet eventually include more lamb? Could that be a side effect of the solar energy revolution? I think the answer is very likely yes,” Slaugh said. “And then when that happens, we’d expect processors and supporting industries to come back, for banks to be willing to give more loans, and for supply chains to follow. All of that grows the economy, and rural economies in particular.”

title: Scientists Discover a New Butterfly Species Hiding in Plain Sight
content:
Butterflies in the genus Colobura are a ubiquitous and familiar sight in Central & South America. For 200 years, this genus was thought to contain a single species. Turns out there were two more hiding in plain sight. Credit: Andrés orellana
Nearly identical butterflies share the same tropical forests, yet scientists still cannot fully explain how they recognize their own kind.
When Andrés Orellana found caterpillars stripping the leaves from a
Cecropia
sapling in Venezuela, they had the familiar black bodies and yellow spines of
Colobura
butterflies. None, however, had the cream-colored markings seen in the two known species.
That missing detail helped lead researchers to a third species,
Colobura cryptica
. Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and her colleagues described the species in
, drawing on genetic evidence and subtle differences in the insects’ appearance. Their work also raised an unresolved question about how these nearly identical butterflies remain separate species while sharing much of the same territory.
Colobura
is a familiar presence in the tropical Americas, or neotropics. These rainforests are among the most biodiverse places on Earth. Costa Rica alone supports half a million species, five times as many as Canada on roughly one two-hundredth of its land area.
“If you go to the neotropics,
Colobura
is one of the first butterflies you see,” Sapkota said.
Colobura butterflies have characteristic zebra-striped wings that makes them easy to recognize and hard to miss. Credit: David Geale
Their caterpillars feed on
Cecropia
, trees as characteristic of these tropical forests as balsam firs are of boreal forests in parts of Canada. In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper wrote, “Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember
Cecropia
, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries.”
Both the butterflies and their host trees occur across a broad area that includes parts of the Andes, the Brazilian Amazon, the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay, and much of Central America and the Caribbean. Most of the 61
Cecropia
species occupy only part of that territory, with some restricted to the Andes and others to the Caribbean. For more than two centuries after Carl Linnaeus’s 1758 description, however, scientists recognized just one widespread species of
Colobura
, called
C. dirce
Caterpillar clues dismissed for 150 years
The caterpillars offered an early reason to question that classification. Their velvety black bodies carry bright yellow stalks tipped with sharp, angled barbs, a warning that roughly translates to “leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences.” Beneath the spines, some have cream-colored teardrops, while others have rings. In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp argued that these different markings distinguished two species. His peers dismissed the idea, and for roughly the next 150 years, naturalists attributed the differences to variation between males and females or among individuals of the same species.
Keith Willmott, now a curator at the Florida Museum’s McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity, later helped revisit that interpretation. He explained why even recognizing a second species had seemed difficult to accept.
Illustration of Colobura and its Cecropia host plant from Jan Sepp’s book on the butterflies of Suriname. Credit: “SURINAAMSCHE VLINDERS : NAAR HET LEVEN GETEEKEND” (1848-1852) BY JAN SEPP, CC0
“It’s a very distinctive butterfly. It’s hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they’re so different from anything else.”
In 2001, Willmott and several colleagues revived Sepp’s idea and
formally described
Colobura annulata
. “We assumed that was the problem solved,” Willmott said. He moved on to other projects.
About a quarter century later, Orellana’s photographs of the unmarked Venezuelan caterpillars gave Willmott enough evidence to reopen the investigation. Orellana was one of his colleagues, and the photographs brought him back to a possibility he had previously set aside. “I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible.”
DNA confirms three nearly identical species
Sapkota had just joined the Florida Museum’s Shirey lab and expressed interest in leading the work. To investigate the butterflies’ genetic relationships, she analyzed highly variable stretches of DNA known as barcodes. These sequences had been collected and curated through a long-term survey of Lepidoptera, the group that includes butterflies and moths, in Costa Rica. Study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs led that survey.
Credit: Florida Museum of Natural History
Building on the barcode results, Sapkota sent older museum specimens collected throughout the neotropics to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. Grishin sequenced their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Together, the DNA analyses identified three distinct lineages that matched the physical differences the researchers documented.
Finding those physical differences in adult butterflies required close inspection. A gray band on the underside of the forewings varied slightly in width and in whether it reached a perpendicular yellow band. After examining preserved specimens for hours, Sapkota also noticed a faint violet glimmer beneath the wings, with a slightly different sheen among some individuals. It made her think of ultraviolet light, which many butterflies can see but humans cannot.
“I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn’t look violet to me, it reflected UV light,” she said.
All three species reflected ultraviolet light at different wavelengths. Beyond the subtle wing-band differences, Sapkota found no other anatomical features that separated the adults. Even their male genitalia were alike, although these structures often provide the most useful anatomical clues for distinguishing moth and butterfly species.
The researchers’ findings provide a simplified guide to telling the three species apart:
Gray wing band broadens slightly and does not touch the yellow transverse band
Average UV reflectance at 376 nanometers (nm)
Cream-colored teardrops on abdominal segments
Gray wing band is uniform in width and touches the yellow transverse band
Average UV reflectance at 370 nm
Cream-colored rings on abdominal segments
Gray wing band is uniform in width and does not touch the yellow transverse band
Average UV reflectance at 344 nm
No cream-colored markings
Those small physical differences might not have justified naming a new species on their own. Their agreement with the three genetic lineages made the case much stronger. The nuclear DNA examined in the study also showed no signs of hybridization, or interbreeding between the species.
Many Cecropia trees are myrmecophytic, meaning they have a mutualistic relationship with ants. The ants live inside the hollow stems of mature trees where they raise Homoptera insects, which siphon sugar from the trees and convert it to honeydew that the ants subsist on. The trees also produce a special type of fat- and protein-rich food the ants consume called Müllerian bodies. In return for the food and a place to live, the ants are generally thought to protect the trees from anything that might try to eat their leaves; possibly as a consequence of this, Colobura caterpillars are often found grazing on saplings, which are much less likely to contain ants than adult trees. Credit: Florida Museum of Natural History
Shared forests, separate species
How the butterflies recognize suitable mates remains unclear. They lack the scent glands that some butterflies and many moths use to release distinctive chemical signals called pheromones, suggesting that visual cues probably play some role. Sapkota is investigating whether the differences in ultraviolet coloration help them choose partners.
Other butterflies and moths, including garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths, have UV-reflecting scales thought to contribute to mate selection. Whether
Colobura
uses those signals in the same way is still uncertain. Sapkota’s ongoing study has so far produced inconclusive results.
The butterflies’ overlapping ranges make their separation especially puzzling.
C. dirce
occupies the largest area, stretching from Mexico to southeastern Brazil and including both sides of the Andes and the Caribbean archipelago.
C. annulata
is similarly widespread but absent from the Greater Antilles.
C. cryptica
has the smallest known range, extending from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.
Sapkota said, “It’s crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time.”
For new species to form, some kind of isolation must limit interbreeding between populations. Biologists think that geographic separation is often responsible. A mountain range, for example, can divide a population into groups that accumulate different traits over time. If they eventually become unable to interbreed even after coming back into contact, they would be considered separate species.
Colobura
researchers suspect that the butterflies may instead gain some separation by occupying different heights within the same forest.
“There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies,” Sapkota said. “
Colobura dirce
is typically found in the undergrowth and
C. cryptica
C. annulata
are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies.”
Some of those conflicting observations may reflect the difficulty of identifying the species, even for experienced butterfly taxonomists. Establishing where each species spends its time will require observations in the forests they share. As Sapkota put it, “Someone has to go to the field to find it out themselves.”
Reference: “Revisiting Colobura (Lepidoptera: Nymphalidae): Using integrative taxonomy to identify a new species, C. cryptica sp. nov., and revise geographic boundaries” by Anisha Sapkota, Andrés Orellana, Nick V. Grishin, Isidro Chacón, Daniel H. Janzen, Winnie Hallwachs, Leina Song, Sajan KC and Keith R. Willmott, 4 May 2026,

title: A Cave Full of Ancient Human Remains Has a Strange Secret: Where Are All the Males?
content:
Rising Star cave system excavation. Credit: Matthew Berger
Ancient tooth proteins raise the possibility that Homo naledi, an extinct human relative, reserved a burial site for females, hinting at complex customs once thought unique to modern humans.
For more than a decade, researchers have wondered why the adult fossils in South Africa’s Dinaledi Chamber look so much alike. The remains of
Homo naledi
, an extinct relative of modern humans, show almost none of the physical variation expected between males and females. Ancient proteins extracted from teeth found in the chamber now suggest a possible explanation: the sampled individuals may all have been female.
The chamber lies within the Rising Star Cave system, where
Homo naledi
was discovered in 2013. The species lived between 335,000 and 241,000 years ago and possessed an unusual combination of primitive, ape-like traits and human-like features.
No male marker in 23 teeth
To investigate the lack of variation, researchers from the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other international institutions recovered the first ancient proteins from
Homo naledi
fossils. Their study, published in
, examined the largest extinct hominin population yet studied through protein analysis.
The team used a minimally destructive acid-etching technique to extract microscopic protein fragments, called peptides, from the enamel of 23 teeth representing at least 20 individuals. They looked for Amelogenin-Y, a protein encoded by a gene on the male Y chromosome, but found no trace of the male marker.
To check that the recovered proteins were genuinely ancient rather than modern contamination, a team at the University of York’s specialized chemistry facility analyzed their amino acids, the molecular building blocks of proteins.
Palesa Madupe, who completed the work as part of her postdoctoral research at the University of Copenhagen, explained why tooth enamel can preserve evidence that other skeletal material may lose.
“Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel – the hardest tissue in the human body – shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.
“This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it’s probably because they could have all belonged to one sex.”
Burial customs or a genetic difference
If the Dinaledi Chamber was a burial site reserved exclusively for females, it could represent the first known example of sex-specific burial by a species other than
Homo sapiens
. Such a practice could imply complex, symbolic treatment of the dead previously thought unique to modern humans, raising questions about how
Homo naledi
organized its society.
Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York’s Department of Chemistry, said, “The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.
“These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins.”
The absence of Amelogenin-Y does not, however, establish that every sampled individual was female. The researchers also identified a possible biological explanation. If the
Homo naledi
population was highly isolated, the gene encoding the protein could have mutated or been deleted. Males could therefore have been present in the chamber, with teeth that lacked the usual male marker.
Reference: “Proteomic analysis of dental enamel from 20 Homo naledi individuals shows no male markers” by Palesa P. Madupe, Alberto J. title: EQCell wins first mass-production order for its perovskite solar electrode deposition tool
content:
EQCell wins first mass-production order for its perovskite solar electrode deposition tool
, a Korean equipment maker whose largest shareholder is Hyulim Robot, has won an order worth about US$7 million (9.3 billion won) for perovskite solar cell manufacturing equipment. The customer is an unnamed global battery and energy company, which EQCell refers to as “C”. It is the first time EQCell’s equipment will be used on a commercial mass-production line.
The equipment is a New Plasma Source System (NPS), which forms the transparent conductive oxide (TCO) electrodes of the solar cells. It is based on reactive plasma deposition, and the company says the low-temperature process limits damage to the underlying materials while depositing the electrode uniformly. EQCell says the tool is designed for ultra-large glass substrates exceeding 1200×2400 mm, larger than the biggest size it says is currently manufacturable. Delivery and on-site installation are scheduled for completion by the first half of 2027.
EQCell had supplied related equipment to a pilot line in 2022, a first R&D line in 2023 and a second R&D line in 2024. These deliveries, it says, helped validate process stability and mass-production yield. The company expects follow-on orders as its customer expands its production facilities.
Based in Suwon, EQCell also makes automation and plasma process equipment for secondary batteries, OLEDs and EMI shielding.

title: A Neocloud’s Gathering Storm
content: Welcome, Weekenders! Whenever I’m the slightest bit ill, I take to my bed and mope. If it goes more than a day or so, I assume the worst—that the end is nigh. I can’t honestly remember the last time I felt unwell for more than a couple days, but I imagine such a scenario would probably find me consulting ChatGPT about burial shrouds. So I’d like to extend a smidgen of sympathy to CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator. Surely, he’s been feeling poorly for nearly two weeks! In the last 12 days, CoreWeave’s stock has been nearly halved. A confluence of factors has contributed to the rampant decline, as my colleague Dakin Campbell explained . In short, investors are worried about how rising interest rates will affect CoreWeave’s ability to raise debt, which it needs to fund its business of selling cloud computing services. They’re also concerned about whether CoreWeave can handle the costs of the mound of debt it already has. Last week, fresh data on U.S. inflation fueled interest rate concerns: Inflation jumped in September, increasing the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates—making all debt more expensive. Even though there was no new inflation data this week, CoreWeave shares continued to fall—from around $60 on Monday to roughly $54 on Friday. Not even Nvidia’s all-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang, was able to stanch the bleeding when he tried to sound a note of confidence for CoreWeave on Thursday, saying the demand for companies like CoreWeave—neoclouds—is “off the charts.” The stock nerds over at Barron’s tried to argue that Wednesday’s earnings report from SpaceX is actually a good sign for CoreWeave. Those numbers showed surging demand for SpaceX’s nascent business of selling its excess AI compute, but I’m not sure whether that necessarily bodes well for the company. Yes, an indicator of demand for compute could be interpreted as a welcome data point for CoreWeave, a compute seller. But SpaceX’s compute business increasingly seems like a real competitor to CoreWeave and other neoclouds, and as the much, much better established company, SpaceX has the resources to fund expansion of its compute-selling efforts without acquiring hazardous amounts of debt. And investors are a great deal less likely to sink its stock price over interest rate jitters. More news from Wednesday highlighted the industry’s appetite for compute. Meta Platforms said it will create a new share class in January—essentially a two-for-one stock split—that will allow it to reach for more capital to spend on AI. It’s also partly a maneuver that would help CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay off California’s billionaire tax if the levy is approved next month. Meta’s board justified helping Zuck pay his taxes by saying that the CEO had threatened to pick up sticks and leave California—and that it was essential to have him in the office as much as possible. (I had to laugh. Just a couple years ago, Zuckerberg was telling us the metaverse would arrive soon , and we’d all be living as digital stick things. Such was the potential of the metaverse that Zuckerberg renamed his entire company for it. Well, guess not!) More capital at Meta might be good for CoreWeave. Meta is a CoreWeave customer —to the tune of $35 billion. There’s no guarantee, of course, that Meta will take a newfound gusher of capital and go back to CoreWeave again. Recently, Meta has been building its own data centers and readying production of its custom AI chips. It has also considered selling compute . Investors looked on wearily at Meta’s stock split/potential Zuck gift, with the company’s shares dropping nearly 9% on Thursday. In fact, Meta’s moves unnerved the entire market yet again over how much this whole AI thing will cost. The Nasdaq sank 2.6% on Thursday. CoreWeave shares fell 10%, while declines also hit Nebius (down 7.2%) and IREN (8.3%), the two other publicly traded neoclouds. And everything kept falling on Friday. Are all the stock moves based on buttoned-up rationality? No. But like the common cold that I’m always certain will put me six feet under, worry on Wall Street is contagious. —Abram Brown ( abe@theinformation.com ) The Information’s Must-Read Stories Ramp Investors Went Nuclear Against Airwallex After Doomed Deal Hackers Used Claude and Grok to Automate Attacks on Banks How CoreWeave’s Debt Binge Brought a Moment of Reckoning Listening: “ Bear Brook: A Private Matter ” Back in 2017, NHPR, a little public radio station in New Hampshire, found itself with a hit national podcast, “Bear Brook,” about cold-case murders—four bodies in two barrels stashed in Bear Brook State Park—and the genetic testing involved in investigating the crimes. Reporter Jason Moon followed up with a second season about a different crime in 2023 and now returns with a third season about another weird happening: the disappearance of 76-year-old Jay Hickey, a local Christmas tree farmer. (Moon likens the setting to a Hallmark movie—frankly, it gave me distinct “Twin Peaks” vibes.) After Hickey vanished one autumn, it was months before anyone went looking for him. That was strange because he was suffering from dementia, so surely his wife, Pat, would’ve, uh, noticed he wasn’t around, right? Obviously she offed him, right? Perhaps, but she clearly was suffering from something herself. It’s the type of tale that could be glossed over with schlock, sordid storytelling. That’s definitely not Moon’s approach. —Abram Brown Reading: “ Kobuk the Destroyer ” by Alex Davies Just in the past 12 hours, I’ve dodged a number of possible catastrophes: I was not singed by my hair dryer, crushed by my office’s elevator doors or left unproductive by a bunch of buttons tumbling out of my keyboard. I owe my good fortune to the rigorous science of product testing, a gorpy-seeming topic made into enlightening, witty entertainment in “Kobuk the Destroyer” by Alex Davies, a former Wired magazine editor. It is an ode to the nerd geniuses who devise those tests, but it can also feel like a drop directly onto the factory floor of Looney Tunes’ Acme Corporation,  presenting a sharp critique of how often executives cut corners and ignore blatant problems as they pursue commercialization. Without the centurylong expansion of product testing, we’d all be left in the same position as Wile E. Coyote, with faulty, rocket-powered roller skates attached to our feet. The titular Kobuk, a grizzly bear, may be one of the most prolific practitioners of the field—having lived out the last several decades at a Montana wildlife sanctuary that partners with a government agency to certify various products as bear proof. Kobuk has the great joy of tearing apart coolers, trash cans, composters, and many other items, and gets rewarded with fish, peanut butter, honey, and dog biscuits for his efforts: Whatever survives Kobuk’s assault receives the certification. Through his efforts, the general public can buy coolers that actually do keep out other Kobuks. Theoretically, that prevents his shaggy-haired brethren from learning to filch food or hang around humans, habits that can get a bear relocated or euthanized. Kobuk has pawed his way onto a noble path initially blazed in the 1920s by Underwriters Laboratories, a Chicago-based business that pioneered the art of product testing—with engineers who assessed the durability of safes by subjecting them to thousand-degree heat, 30-foot drops and kerosene-fueled explosions. Davies keeps up a brisk pace as he winds through the many testing approaches adopted by various industries in the following years, including the NASA wind tunnel used to develop the Curiosity Mars lander and the oval-shaped gelatin sacks that engineers fired into airplane engines to avoid needing to kill thousands and thousands of live birds. As many of you might surely agree, determining the safety of one group of products in particular remains decidedly challenging: ahem, AI! Much of the alignment training and red teaming that goes into AI development comes away with vague conclusions, Davies writes: We simply don’t understand enough about what we’ve created, and AI often operates much more unpredictably than, say, a refrigerator door or an airbag. Trying to understand why an AI behaved safely in one setting but dangerously in another is “like trying to understand why your dog growls at people carrying shopping bags but not people carrying suitcases.” —A.B. Watching: “ Carrie ” Stephen King’s cabinet of terrors is a well-stocked place, cluttered with weird evils, many with complex, lengthy backstories. The It of “It,” you may recall, is not actually an evil clown—it’s an ageless, alien ball of light. “The Langoliers” is a time-travel story…about piranha-like, interdimensional critters that literally eat time. I could try to also get into the motivations of Randall Flagg in “The Stand,” but unlike King, I don’t have 823 pages to do that here. The knottier of King’s novels defy easy screen adaptations. Other retellings of King stories fail on the screen largely because they suffer in comparison to finer, earlier movie adaptations, to say nothing of their misappropriation of King’s material. On Amazon, there’s an excellent new restructuring of King’s “Carrie,” his first bestseller and, of course, the source for a much-loved film by director Brian De Palma, which put both De Palma and King on the map. There’s a simplicity and universal resonance to King’s story of tortured, telekinetic high schooler Carrie White that makes it highly moldable: Teenagers have been terrifying ever since there have been teenagers, both to themselves and to those around them. Amazon’s “Carrie” was helmed by Mike Flanagan, who has a string of spooky series on Netflix (“The Fall of the House of Usher,” “The Haunting of Hill House”) and did the 2019 movie adaptation of King’s “Doctor Sleep.” Flanagan adeptly positions his “Carrie” in the modern day. The infamous shower scene, for example, does not really end when Carrie (newcomer Summer Howell) is escorted away by kindhearted PE teacher Miss Desjardin (Amber Midthunder). Her bullying classmates captured the entire thing on their cellphones, and their torment of her continues via an anonymous Instagram account. Later, her mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), a religious nut who also favors QAnon-like conspiracy theories, seizes the internet as a means for her own ferocious manipulations. With the benefit of an eight-episode run, Flanagan gets the opportunity to give greater depth to the Whites and the people around them, including Carrie’s chief bully, Christine (Alison Thornton), and classmate Sue (Siena Agudong), who befriends Carrie in this version. Granted, it might seem like Flanagan is trying to stretch the material as thin as a funeral crepe. He doesn’t, aided by roundly top-notch performances. —A.B.

title: Anthropic’s Margin is OpenAI’s Opportunity
content: OpenAI’s efforts to undercut Anthropic on price are producing some results. For instance, in May, Anthropic models powered 57% of the coding work of hundreds of engineers at Rippling, an HR software firm, while OpenAI models handled 16% of that work. Since then, the situation has reversed: 52% of the coding work is now handled by OpenAI models and 18% with Anthropic ones, as the company sought to cut costs and OpenAI proved cheaper, CEO Parker Conrad said. “Anyone who is smart and sophisticated about this over the summer was trying to dramatically cut back from Anthropic and switch to other tools,” Conrad said, though he didn’t provide specifics. Other sophisticated startups are making similar moves. Replit, a coding app, in recent months switched the majority of its AI spending to OpenAI from Anthropic after OpenAI offered a discount of more than 30% on its model prices as part of a contract worth more than $100 million annually, according to a person familiar with the situation. The startup had planned to stick with Anthropic, but Anthropic wouldn’t extend a discount it had previously provided to Replit unless the startup committed to a higher spending level, this person said. (Replit has publicly discussed shifting toward OpenAI but hasn’t disclosed the discount it is receiving nor the size of the contract.) Investors will be looking closely at the impact of OpenAI and freely available open source models on Anthropic’s growth rate as it prepares for a blockbuster initial public offering as soon as next month. That rate slowed materially between the second and third quarters , though it was still extraordinarily high, at 45%. Another potential growth factor: Some of Anthropic’s biggest customers, including Cognition, Meta and Microsoft, are developing their own technologies and other alternatives to reduce spending on Claude. Parker Conrad, CEO of Rippling. Photo by Betty Laura Zapata/Getty Images In recent months, OpenAI appears to have drawn some customers from Anthropic by offering heavy discounts and other freebies for both its coding tool, Codex, and models that businesses can buy using application programming interfaces. The moves came after Anthropic, based on the strength of its models for coding, leapfrogged OpenAI in revenue during the second quarter and was about 50% bigger in terms of revenue over the summer. OpenAI has said its enterprise revenue growth accelerated in recent months, though reliable data are hard to come by. Data from corporate spending software provider Ramp , which is used by many startups, shows Anthropic adoption surged in the second quarter and overtook OpenAI, as a percentage of Ramp customers, and the two are now neck and neck. Higher Margins Just as important as market share, Anthropic’s pricing power means it has had high gross profit margins compared to OpenAI . Anthropic spent just $5.6 billion on computing costs in the second quarter, including costs to develop new models, less than half the $11.5 billion in revenue it generated, The Information previously reported. Meanwhile, OpenAI previously projected it would spend significantly more on compute costs than the revenue it expects to generate this year. That means OpenAI’s discounts may be buying market share at the expense of already-negative margins. Anthropic has continued to operate as if it isn’t threatened. While both Anthropic and archrival OpenAI provide discounts to customers that spend millions of dollars a year on their products, Anthropic has taken the unusual step of ending customers’ discounts once they hit usage limits in their contracts, The Information has reported . That policy appears to have cost Anthropic Replit’s business. Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit. Photo by Betty Laura Zapata/Getty Images That has opened the door for OpenAI, which in recent months launched new models that were more competitive with Anthropic’s than its prior ones, many app developers say. Heavy users of such models say it’s a relative cinch to switch providers. For instance, Replit took mere hours to make code changes to switch to OpenAI models from Anthropic’s, and just a few days to make the changes to its products, a faster turnaround than the time it took Replit to negotiate the earlier Anthropic contract, said the person with knowledge of the situation. Anthropic Strikes Back This dynamic also means Anthropic could win back some of the business it lost if it launches better models. That may have already occurred. A month ago, OpenAI overtook Anthropic to become the most-used model provider to customers of OpenRouter, a service that businesses use to access different models through a single vendor. But after Anthropic launched its Claude Opus 5.5 model late last month, it retook the lead and was twice as popular as OpenAI models over the last week or so, OpenRouter said. (Anthropic is now preparing to release a model that reads users’ intentions better , while OpenAI is scrambling to release a powerful new flagship model without taking too many safety and security risks.) In some cases, OpenAI is taking small bites of the budgets of loyal Anthropic customers. Vijay Rayapati, the CEO of Atomicwork, which automates IT support tickets, said his company has begun training new engineers to use Codex rather than Claude Code because of free credits it has received from both OpenAI and from its venture capital firm. That VC firm, Khosla Ventures, is a major OpenAI investor that offers such credits to startups in its investment portfolio, according to a person familiar with the situation. While Atomicwork plans to spend around $2 million on Claude Code in the current fiscal year that ends January next year, Rayapati anticipates the startup will spend nearly $300,000 on Codex in the same period, compared to spending almost nothing on that product in the prior year. Atomicwork CEO Vijay Rayapati, credit: Helen Shanthi, Atomicwork. OpenAI has been more available to help some customers use Codex effectively, some founders say. For example, one startup backed by Andreessen Horowitz, which has invested in OpenAI, says they are in a Slack group chat with OpenAI engineers and salespeople to help resolve issues with the coding tool when they arise. Anthropic did not make engineers available to the startup in a similar group message with sales reps from that company. Huge Discounts OpenAI recently has floated discounts higher than the 20% to 30% that some founders said they received on listed prices for its models. For example, Jonathan Cornelissen, CEO of workforce training firm DataCamp, which has about 200 employees and is a big spender on Anthropic models, says OpenAI has offered 40% off models that DataCamp uses internally to develop products. To get the discount, the startup must agree to also use Codex rather than a competing tool like OpenCode or Claude Code. While weighing that offer, DataCamp is also negotiating to apply the same discount to OpenAI models—which are cheaper than Anthropic’s, before the discount—that power an application the startup sells to its customers, he said. Such a change would result in “significant” savings and higher gross margins, he said. “We’re looking at an 80% to 90% decrease in costs,” Cornelissen said. “It’s huge.” OpenAI is also trying to keep existing customers from looking at Claude. For instance, it recently allowed an American bank that has more than $7 billion in assets to double its ChatGPT accounts to 500 workers, without raising the annual contract cost of around $40,000, according to an executive at that firm. (That would amount to less than $7 per month per worker, an extraordinary discount from the typical price of more than $20 per month per worker.) The firm’s marketing teams use ChatGPT to generate ads and its HR staffers use it to create job descriptions for new roles, but it was starting to consider switching some of that work to Claude before OpenAI sweetened its contract, the executive said.

title: Instacart Is Exploring a Sale
content: Instacart is in talks to sell itself in a transaction that would cap the grocery delivery app’s 14-year run as a standalone company. Currently valued at $12 billion, Instacart has been working with an investment bank to weigh its options and held at least preliminary conversations with DoorDash and Uber, according to people familiar with the matter, though talks with Uber are not ongoing, according to a person close to Uber. The potential buyer would acquire one of Silicon Valley’s best known consumer companies, which became a lifeline for many Americans during the Covid-19 lockdown. There’s no guarantee Instacart’s talks to sell itself will lead to a deal.  A typical takeover premium of 30% to 40% would value Instacart at roughly $16 billion to $17 billion, based on recent public tech deals. Instacart shares rose 10% in Friday regular trading after the report. A bid for Instacart would likely invite antitrust scrutiny, however, given the overlap between its operations and those of possible acquirers such as DoorDash and Uber, both of which also offer grocery delivery. The Trump administration’s antitrust enforcers have been more willing to approve acquisitions with conditions, such as requiring certain business divestitures, though a combination of direct rivals would still face an investigation. Instacart has long been speculated as a potential acquisition target for Uber, which has a $135 billion market cap, and DoorDash, whose market cap is roughly $80 billion. Instacart has had closer business ties to Uber in recent years , including a partnership in which customers could order restaurant delivery from Uber Eats through the Instacart app. Uber executives have  also had several conversations with Instacart over the years, according to people involved with them. But they didn’t progress as Uber focused on other acquisitions, which have ranged from Postmates in 2020 to Delivery Hero this year. In 2021, Instacart, then valued privately at $39 billion, held talks with DoorDash on a potential sale that would value the grocery-delivery firm between $40 billion and $50 billion, The Information reported . The talks fell apart, at least partly due to questions about whether a combination could get approval from antitrust regulators during the Biden administration. Instacart went public in 2023 at a valuation of $10 billion, after the end of the pandemic slowed its past torrid growth, lowering its valuation. Shares have risen 70% from the IPO price. Since going public, the Instacart’s growth has paled in comparison to its larger rivals, despite a high-profile move into selling ads. Instacart’s annual revenue growth slowed to 11% for both 2024 and 2025, compared to 19% in 2023. In comparison, DoorDash’s revenue rose 28% in 2025 from the prior year, while revenues at Uber, which also includes a substantial ride-hailing business, rose 18% over that same period. Another factor that may be constraining Instacart’s growth: Amazon. The ecommerce giant has continually expanded its grocery delivery efforts, especially after its acquisition of Whole Foods nearly a decade ago. On the bright side, Instacart has been consistently generating cash in recent quarters and its growth has ticked up this year. In the second quarter this year, for instance, Instacart revenue rose 14% to $1 billion, and it generated $480 million in free cash flow. The company has said it’s using a majority of its free cash flows this year to buy back its shares, which have risen 16% so far this year. Uber and DoorDash have been busy consolidating the food-delivery market in recent years. DoorDash bought European food delivery service Wolt in 2022 for about $8 billion, and it purchased British delivery service Deliveroo and restaurant software company SevenRooms last year. Uber’s activities this year could make it more difficult to pursue another large-scale deal with Instacart. In recent months, Uber struck deals to buy European firm Delivery Hero for around $15 billion and workplace food-catering service ezCater for more than $2 billion.

title: 科学网-减少重复开发和建设成本，我国启动自主实验室标准体系研制工作
content:
减少重复开发和建设成本，我国启动自主实验室标准体系研制工作
记者今天了解到，中国标准化研究院近日发布《自主实验室标准体系前瞻框架与实施路线报告（2026）》，首次提出自主实验室标准体系前瞻框架与分阶段实施路线。
什么是自主实验室？
简单来说，就是让人工智能当“大脑”，让机器人和自动化实验设备当“四肢”，从实验设计到具体操作、结果分析，都可以在人工智能的辅助下完成，并根据实验结果不断改进下一步实验。这有望帮助科学家减少重复性工作，更快验证新想法。
如今，自主实验室正成为人工智能助力科学研究的重要方向。美国、英国、德国等国家已经在材料研发、药物发现等领域开展相关探索。但要让这些技术走出少数示范实验室、得到更广泛应用，还有一个现实难题：不同厂家的仪器设备和软件往往“各说各话”，数据格式不一致，连接起来费时费力。目前国际上相关标准化工作已起步，但统一、完善的标准体系仍有待建立。
为解决这些问题，《报告》提出了自主实验室标准体系建设框架。中国标准化研究院正联合有关高校、科研机构和企业，围绕实验室术语、设备接口、实验数据等方面推进我国标准研究和研制，让不同设备和软件有共同的“语言”和“规则”，更方便地连接和协同工作，实验数据更易共享与追溯，减少重复开发和建设成本。这将为提高科研效率、推动不同实验室之间的合作提供支持，促进自主实验室从示范探索走向更广泛应用。

title: 科学网-美航空航天局公布“阿耳忒弥斯3号”任务最新安排
content:
美航空航天局公布“阿耳忒弥斯3号”任务最新安排
美国航空航天局（资料图）
美国航空航天局23日公布“阿耳忒弥斯3号”任务最新安排。按计划，该任务将于2027年把4名宇航员送入近地轨道，先后与美国蓝色起源公司和太空探索技术公司研制的登月系统测试飞行器开展交会对接等测试，为后续“阿耳忒弥斯4号”载人登月任务做准备。
据介绍，“阿耳忒弥斯3号”任务计划持续14天，将使用3枚不同的运载火箭，分别将蓝色起源公司研发的“蓝月Mark 2”号月球着陆器测试版、“猎户座”载人飞船和“星舰”测试飞行器送入太空。任务旨在验证不同航天器在轨协同工作的能力，演练交会、对接、舱内操作等关键程序，降低未来载人登月的风险。
按计划，“蓝月Mark 2”号着陆器测试版将率先发射，进入近地轨道并在轨检查。在确认其状态良好、具备联合运行条件后，美航空航天局将在数天内使用新一代登月火箭“太空发射系统”发射搭载4名宇航员的“猎户座”飞船。飞船入轨后将调整轨道，与等待中的“蓝月”对接。宇航员计划进入“蓝月Mark 2”号停留约2天，评估舱内环境、控制装置以及生命保障系统等。任务团队将验证该着陆器维持适宜大气环境和气压的能力。
完成相关测试后，“猎户座”飞船将与“蓝月Mark 2”号分离。太空探索技术公司计划从佛罗里达州发射“星舰”V3测试飞行器，随后“猎户座”将与其交会对接，测试时间最长约2小时，宇航员不会进入“星舰”。这一阶段主要验证航天器对接后的协同运行能力，评估飞行器可控性、通信能力、软件协同及对接和分离操作。
美航空航天局表示，任务期间还将测试宇航员的宇航服、对接传感器等设备，评估飞船热环境，并进行宇航员健康评估、细胞生物学实验以及地球和太阳观测等活动，还将测试把月球样本带回地球的相关方案。任务结束后，“猎户座”飞船将搭载宇航员返回地球，在加利福尼亚州附近海域溅落。
今年2月，美航空航天局宣布调整“阿耳忒弥斯”登月计划架构，将“阿耳忒弥斯3号”任务改为在近地轨道进行系统及运行能力测试，将原计划于2027年实施的首次载人登月任务调整为“阿耳忒弥斯4号”，推迟至2028年实施。
